Euler–Poinsot motion, torque-free nutation and the intermediate axis · Analytical mechanics from constraints to invariants

A freely rotating body has fixed angular momentum in space, yet the components recorded by three body-mounted gyroscopes can vary periodically or linger near an unstable rotation. Solve the nonsymmetric top from its invariants, distinguish its body-component period from its spatial orientation, and extract a stability time scale from a measured inertia tensor.

Chapter 10 · Forced, damped vibration

Use amplitude, phase and power together to estimate the mechanical properties of an oscillator from a sinusoidal drive.

From first principles

Derive the steady amplitude and its phase lag

The force laws for a simple vibration test are an elastic restoring force \(-kx\), a viscous force \(-c\dot x\) and a prescribed drive \(F_0\cos\omega t\). Newton's law gives

\[m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=F_0\cos\omega t.\]

Assume linear coefficients, positive damping and enough time for the free transient to decay. Seek the response at the measured drive frequency by setting \(x=\operatorname{Re}(Xe^{i\omega t})\). Each differentiation multiplies the complex amplitude by \(i\omega\), so

\[(k-m\omega^2+ic\omega)X=F_0 .\]

The magnitude of the complex denominator fixes the measured displacement amplitude; its argument gives the lag of the response relative to the applied force:

\[|X|=\frac{F_0}{\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+c^2\omega^2}},\]
\[\delta=\operatorname{atan2}(c\omega,k-m\omega^2).\]

At low frequency the spring supports nearly the entire force and the displacement approaches \(F_0/k\). At \(\omega=\sqrt{k/m}\) the spring and inertia terms cancel, leaving a quarter-period displacement lag. Multiplying velocity by force and averaging distinguishes this condition of maximum absorbed power from the maximum displacement amplitude.

Derivation and applications

Read the exact mechanical bandwidth from absorbed power

A measured displacement peak need not occur at the frequency of maximum energy absorption. Consider a linear oscillator of mass \(m\), stiffness \(k\) and viscous damping coefficient \(c>0\), driven steadily by \(F_0\cos\omega t\). Let \(X\) denote the complex displacement amplitude. Work over a complete period supplies the energy dissipated by the damper, whose instantaneous loss is \(c\dot x^2\). Since the velocity amplitude is \(\omega|X|\), averaging its square gives

\[\overline P=\tfrac12 c\omega^2 |X|^2=\frac{c F_0^2\omega^2/2}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+c^2\omega^2}.\]

Divide numerator and denominator by \(\omega^2\). The frequency-dependent term in the denominator becomes \((k/\omega-m\omega)^2\), which vanishes exactly at \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\). Hence \(\overline P_{\max}=F_0^2/(2c)\). The half-power condition is particularly simple:

\[|k-m\omega^2|=c\omega .\]

There are two positive roots, one on each side of \(\omega_0\). Solving the two quadratics separately yields

\[\omega_\pm=\frac{\sqrt{c^2+4mk}\pm c}{2m},\]
\[\omega_+-\omega_-=\frac cm,\]
\[\omega_+\omega_-=\frac km .\]

The half-power bandwidth in angular-frequency units is exactly \(c/m\) for this viscously damped, constant-force experiment. For weak damping the frequencies become nearly symmetric around \(\omega_0\). In stronger damping the geometric mean still gives \(\omega_0\). The frequencies correspond to half the peak power, equivalently to the velocity amplitude falling to \(1/\sqrt2\) of its maximum.

Worked example

Plan the frequency sweep for a test fixture

Change the inputs and investigate this derivation.

For \(m=0.400\) kg, \(k=160\) N/m and \(c=4.00\) N s/m, the peak lies at \(20.0\) rad/s. The half-power edges are \(15.62\) and \(25.62\) rad/s, about \(2.49\) and \(4.08\) Hz. A force amplitude \(F_0=2.00\) N produces \(0.500\) W at resonance and \(0.250\) W at either edge. The peak displacement occurs at a slightly lower frequency, so a displacement maximum alone would give a different estimate.

Second application

Recover a stiffness without measuring the peak height

Change the inputs and investigate this derivation.

A \(0.250\) kg resonator has measured half-power edges at \(3.00\) and \(4.00\) Hz. Convert to radians per second before using the formulas. The damping is \(m\,2\pi(4-3)=1.57\) N s/m; the stiffness is

\[m(2\pi)^2(3)(4)=118\,\mathrm{N/m}.\]

The peak-power frequency predicted from the product is

\[\sqrt{12}=3.46\,\mathrm{Hz}.\]

These estimates do not require calibrating the force amplitude, provided it was constant across the sweep.

OneSimulation laboratory

When does a released mass cross equilibrium?

Release a 1 kg mass from rest 10 mm to the right of equilibrium on a spring of stiffness 4 N/m. A viscous damper exerts a force opposite to the velocity. In a driven machine this free response is the transient left by the initial displacement. Here the external drive is zero, so the transient can be measured on its own.

Predict a crossing. With displacement measured from static equilibrium, the weight has already been balanced. Newton’s second law gives one restoring term for displacement and one for velocity. Write the trial motion as an exponential. Dividing the resulting equation by the nonzero exponential leaves a quadratic:

\[m\ddot x=-kx-c\dot x,\]
\[x=Ae^{st}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s^2+2\zeta\omega_n s+\omega_n^2=0,\]
\[\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m},\]
\[\zeta=\frac{c}{2\sqrt{mk}}.\]

Here \(\omega_n=2\) rad/s. At \(\zeta=0.2\) the roots are \(-0.4\pm1.960i\) s⁻¹. The imaginary part permits a zero crossing. At critical damping the double root is \(-2\) s⁻¹. Applying the initial conditions to the two independent solutions gives \(x=10(1+2t)e^{-2t}\) mm. At \(\zeta=2\) the slowest root is about \(-0.536\) s⁻¹. Which of the last two releases is closer to equilibrium at three seconds?

Download this run (CSV)

Read the comparison. At three seconds the critical solution is about 0.174 mm from equilibrium. Increasing damping again leaves about 2.16 mm. The slower real root explains the long tail. The underdamped trajectory has already crossed the equilibrium. The points come from integrating the two first-order equations for displacement and velocity. The line comes from their characteristic roots.

Try a fourth case. Change the damping ratio to 0.7. Predict the first zero from the damped frequency and the phase fixed by release from rest, then find the first sign change in the output CSV.

Further reading · MIT 18.03, Natural frequency and damping ratio.

Download the OneSimulation model (Python). Set up the local runtime, then run the downloaded file:

python oscillator.py --ratio 0.7

Separate the transient from the driven motion

A shaker applies a sinusoidal force to a mass on a spring and viscous damper. Its displacement can lag the force and can remain large even when the applied force is small. Assume motion about a stable equilibrium, constant stiffness \(k\), positive damping coefficient \(c\) and drive \(F_0\cos\omega t\). Newton’s equation is

\[m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=F_0\cos\omega t.\]

The solution contains a homogeneous contribution set by preparation and a particular response set by the continuing drive.

Positive damping makes the homogeneous part decay. To estimate the steady frequency response, measurements must last several decay times at each frequency. Measurements taken immediately after the drive changes include residual free motion. Close to weakly damped resonance that settling time can span many oscillations, so sweeping too rapidly can shift the apparent location of a peak.

Solve for amplitude and lag

Write the steady displacement as the real part of \(Xe^{i\omega t}\) and take \(F_0\) real. Substituting gives

\[X=F_0/(k-m\omega^2+ic\omega).\]

The denominator groups the elastic and inertial contributions along the real axis and viscous loading in quadrature. Its magnitude gives

\[|X|=\frac{F_0}{\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+c^2\omega^2}}.\]

The lag angle is the argument of the denominator, evaluated in the appropriate quadrant. At low frequency \(X\simeq F_0/k\), in phase with force. At high frequency \(X\simeq-F_0/(m\omega^2)\), nearly opposite in phase. At \(\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}\) the reactive terms cancel and the displacement lags by a quarter cycle. This phase condition identifies the undamped natural frequency even when the amplitude maximum lies slightly lower.

Connect absorbed power to damping

Multiply the equation by \(\dot x\) and average over one settled cycle. Both stored kinetic and elastic energies return to their initial values, so the mean input power is dissipated by the damper. For peak displacement,

\[\langle P\rangle=c\omega^2|X|^2/2.\]

At \(\omega_n\), the velocity is in phase with force, giving \(\langle P\rangle=F_0^2/(2c)\). Minimising the denominator of the displacement response gives a different frequency, \(\omega_{\rm peak}^2=k/m-c^2/(2m^2)\), if this is positive. A reported “resonance frequency” should identify the measured observable.

A power scan near a lightly damped resonance has a narrow peak whose half-power bandwidth is approximately \(c/m\) in rad/s. The damping estimate obtained from that width can be compared with an independent ring-down estimate. Significant disagreement could indicate an amplitude-dependent damper or loss in the drive system.

Read a frequency-response experiment

Take \(m=2.0\) kg, \(k=800\) N/m, \(c=8.0\) N·s/m and \(F_0=4.0\) N. The low-frequency displacement is 5.0 mm. At 20 rad/s the displacement is 25 mm, the velocity amplitude is 0.50 m/s and the mean power is 1.0 W. The displacement maximum occurs near \(\sqrt{400-8}=19.8\) rad/s. A run at a single frequency near the peak cannot identify all three parameters. A low-frequency measurement constrains stiffness, the quarter-cycle lag constrains mass relative to stiffness and the absorbed power at that frequency constrains damping independently.

Motion imposed at the support

A vibration mount is often driven through a moving base rather than by a calibrated force on the mass. Let \(y(t)\) be the prescribed absolute displacement of the support and \(x(t)\) the absolute displacement of a supported mass \(m\). A spring and a viscous damper both connect mass to base, so they respond to \(x-y\) and \(\dot x-\dot y\). Newton’s equation is

\[m\ddot x+c(\dot x-\dot y)+k(x-y)=0.\]

The same mass and stiffness as in a force-driven oscillator can therefore produce a different transfer function because the input enters both elastic and dissipative forces.

For harmonic motion proportional to \(e^{i\omega t}\) rearrange the amplitude equation to give

\[(k-m\omega^2+i c\omega)X=(k+i c\omega)Y.\]

Set \(r=\omega/\omega_n\), \(\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}\) and \(\zeta=c/(2m\omega_n)\). The ratio of absolute displacement amplitudes is

\[\left|\frac XY\right|^2=\frac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}.\]

At very low frequencies the mass follows the support almost rigidly. To have \(|X|<|Y|\) requires \((1-r^2)^2>1\), which for positive frequency means \(r>\sqrt2\). Increasing damping reduces the resonant peak but increases the high-frequency path through which the moving support can exert a force. Damping is therefore a design variable with different consequences in different frequency bands.

Check both isolation and suspension travel

A 5.00 kg optical instrument sits on springs with total stiffness \(2000\) N/m and damping ratio \(0.10\). Its natural angular frequency is \(20.0\) rad/s and viscous coefficient \(c=2\zeta m\omega_n=20.0\) N s/m. A nearby machine imposes a sinusoidal base motion of amplitude \(0.800\) mm at \(60.0\) rad/s. Here \(r=3.00\) and \(2\zeta r=0.600\), giving \(|X/Y|=\sqrt{1.36/64.36}=0.145\). The instrument moves through an absolute amplitude of \(0.116\) mm.

The suspension itself accommodates relative displacement. Subtract \(Y\) from \(X\) in the complex equation before taking a magnitude. This gives

\[|(X-Y)/Y|=r^2/\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}=1.12.\]

The spring travel is therefore about \(0.898\) mm, exceeding the base amplitude despite successful instrument isolation. Subtracting the two absolute amplitudes directly would ignore phase and underpredict travel. At twice the damping ratio the same calculation gives \(|X/Y|=0.193\), so high-frequency isolation degrades even as resonance becomes less dangerous. Two simultaneous position sensors, on base and instrument, allow both absolute response and relative travel to be assessed.

A common practical constraint is allowable acceleration rather than displacement. In a sinusoidal test absolute acceleration has amplitude \(\omega^2|X|\). For the stated 60 rad/s motion the mount gives an instrument acceleration of \(3600\times0.000116=0.418\) m/s². The bare base acceleration is \(2.88\) m/s², so the ratio is the same as the displacement ratio at that particular frequency. Across a sweep the factor \(\omega^2\) changes. A decreasing displacement curve therefore does not guarantee a decreasing absolute acceleration, especially if the operational environment has a roughly constant displacement excitation over its upper frequency band.

Mechanical stops add a further check on the model. Once the relative travel reaches a stop, the constraint changes within each cycle, producing harmonics absent from the linear solution. A distorted accelerometer trace can therefore identify a travel problem before mean isolation performance is assessed.

Problem sheet 5 · Rotation, damping and frequency measurements

Use frequency and phase measurements to separate moments of inertia, damping, and static stiffness.

The wobble seen from a rotor

A torque-free symmetric rotor has \(I_1=I_2=0.024\) kg m², \(I_3=0.030\) kg m² and axial angular velocity \(100\) rad/s. Find the frequency of the transverse angular-velocity components in body coordinates. For an instantaneous transverse speed of 4 rad/s, find the angle between the symmetry axis and angular momentum and the inertial precession rate.

Show both frame calculations

Euler’s transverse equations give \(\Omega_b=(I_3-I_1)\omega_3/I_1=25\) rad/s or \(3.98\) Hz. Angular momentum has transverse and axial components \(0.096\) and \(3.00\) kg m²/s. Therefore

\[\theta=\arctan(0.096/3)=1.83^\circ.\]

The body axis follows \(\dot{\mathbf e}_3=(\mathbf L/I_1)\times\mathbf e_3\), so its azimuth about fixed angular momentum advances at \(|\mathbf L|/I_1=125.1\) rad/s. A body-mounted sensor and an external camera measure different rotations.

Read damping from the ring-down

A 0.50 kg oscillator completes ten free cycles in 2.00 s. Its peak displacement decreases from 8.0 to 4.0 mm. Infer the viscous damping coefficient and the spring stiffness. Predict the displacement amplitude under a sinusoidal force of 0.080 N at the undamped natural frequency.

Show the ring-down and driven response

Write the envelope as \(A_0e^{-\gamma t}\). Then \(\gamma=\ln2/2=0.3466\) s⁻¹ and \(c=2m\gamma=0.3466\) N s/m. The damped frequency is \(\omega_d=2\pi(10/2)=31.416\) rad/s, so

\[k=m(\omega_d^2+\gamma^2)=493.5\,\mathrm{N/m}.\]

At \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\) the elastic and inertial terms cancel in the complex response. The amplitude is \(F_0/(c\omega_0)=7.35\) mm and the force leads displacement by a quarter cycle.

Distinguish two mechanical faults

A driven instrument has calibrated mass 1.0 kg and static deflection 1.0 mm under a 1.0 N load. During operation the displacement lags the drive by \(45^\circ\) at 5.0 Hz. Infer viscous damping and predict what changes in static deflection and quadrature frequency if damping doubles.

Show the inference and diagnosis

Static response gives \(k=1000\) N/m. On the low-frequency side \(\tan\delta=c\omega/(k-m\omega^2)\). At \(31.416\) rad/s the elastic excess is \(13.04\) N/m, giving \(c=0.415\) N s/m. At exact quadrature \(k=m\omega^2\), so \(f=5.033\) Hz for both damping values. Static deflection is also unchanged, since the damper exerts no force at rest. Doubling damping halves the displacement at quadrature and widens the response. A stiffness change would instead shift both independent calibration observables.

Test whether a steady precession exists

At tilt \(60^\circ\) a top has \(m=0.300\) kg, \(\ell=0.0400\) m, \(I_1=0.00200\) kg m² and \(I_3=0.00100\) kg m². Find the minimum axial spin for a tilted steady precession. At axial spin 60.0 rad/s estimate the slow rate and compare it with the full solution.

Inspect the discriminant and select the slow root

Real roots require \(I_3^2\omega_3^2\ge4I_1mg\ell\cos\theta\). With \(mg\ell=0.11772\) N m the threshold is \(21.7\) rad/s. Rapid-spin balance gives

\[0.11772/0.0600=1.96\,\mathrm{rad/s}.\]

The lower root of \(0.00100\Omega^2-0.0600\Omega+0.11772=0\) is \(2.03\) rad/s. Below threshold the equations exclude steady rotation at the stipulated tilt. They still allow motion with changing tilt.

Chapter 11 · Nonlinear stiffness and amplitude-dependent period

Derive the leading frequency shift of a symmetric nonlinear oscillator and test whether a measured amplitude shift is consistent with a cubic spring.

From first principles

Derive the first amplitude correction to a spring’s frequency

A symmetric elastic restoring force has no quadratic displacement term; the first correction to a linear spring can therefore be cubic. Suppose a conservative oscillator satisfies \(m\ddot x+kx+\alpha x^3=0\) with \(k>0\) and \(|\alpha A^2/k|\ll1\) at measured peak amplitude \(A\). Leading motion is approximately \(A\cos\Omega t\). Cube this motion to find which frequencies enter the perturbing force:

\[x^3\simeq A^3[\tfrac34\cos\Omega t+\tfrac14\cos3\Omega t] .\]

To maintain a bounded periodic solution, its fundamental component must balance at first order. Otherwise the remaining fundamental force would resonantly grow the correction. Combine the inertia and restoring-force coefficients at \(\cos\Omega t\):

\[-m\Omega^2A+kA+\tfrac34\alpha A^3\simeq0,\qquad \Omega\simeq\sqrt{k/m}\left(1+\frac{3\alpha A^2}{8k}\right).\]

The third-harmonic component also distorts the waveform, but reinserting that order-\(\alpha\) distortion into the cubic force affects the fundamental only at the next perturbative order. Positive \(\alpha\) raises frequency with amplitude; negative \(\alpha\) lowers it within the local range where the stable weakly nonlinear model applies.

Derivation and applications

Find the third harmonic generated by a weak cubic spring

A change in oscillation period is one signature of a nonlinear restoring force. The same nonlinearity also changes the shape of the recorded motion. Let an undamped mass obey \(m\ddot x+kx+\alpha x^3=0\), with \(k>0\). Release it from rest at the measured peak displacement \(A\). Define \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\), the small signed parameter \(\epsilon=\alpha A^2/k\), and a stretched time \(\tau=\Omega t\). Write \(x/A=\cos\tau+\epsilon u(\tau)\) with \(u(0)=u'(0)=0\) so that \(A\) remains the physical turning point.

Allow the frequency to shift as \(\Omega=\omega_0(1+\epsilon\nu)\). Substitute the expansion into the equation and retain terms only to first order in \(\epsilon\). Primes below denote differentiation with respect to \(\tau\):

\[u''+u=2\nu\cos\tau-\cos^3\tau=(2\nu-3/4)\cos\tau-\tfrac14\cos3\tau .\]

A term driven at the unit frequency would grow proportionally to \(\tau\sin\tau\), contradicting a bounded, periodic correction. Choose \(\nu=3/8\) to remove it. The remaining forcing is at three times the fundamental. A trial \(C\cos3\tau\) has \(u''+u=-8C\cos3\tau\). Add the required homogeneous term to satisfy the turning-point conditions:

\[u(\tau)=\frac{\cos3\tau-\cos\tau}{32}.\]

The predicted displacement therefore contains two lines with linked amplitudes and a shifted fundamental:

\[x(t)\simeq A\!\left[(1-\epsilon/32)\cos\Omega t+(\epsilon/32)\cos3\Omega t\right],\qquad \Omega/\omega_0\simeq1+3\epsilon/8 .\]

The coefficient sign gives the third harmonic relative to the phase of a release at positive displacement. Squaring an amplitude to obtain a power spectrum erases that sign. The approximation assumes \(|\epsilon|\ll1\) and excludes appreciable dissipation during the observation.

Worked example

Estimate a micrometre-scale distortion

Change the inputs and investigate this derivation.

Take \(A=12.0\) mm, \(k=20.0\) N/m and \(\alpha=1.00\times10^4\) N/m³. Then \(\epsilon=0.0720\), so the third-harmonic displacement amplitude is

\[12.0(0.0720)/32=0.0270\,\mathrm{mm}.\]

The fundamental frequency should increase by \(2.70\%\). With \(\omega_0=10.0\) rad/s, the third-harmonic line lies close to \(30.8\) rad/s.

Second application

Test whether a measured line comes from the spring

Change the inputs and investigate this derivation.

At \(A=6.00\) mm on the same apparatus, \(\epsilon\) falls by four and the third-harmonic amplitude falls by eight to \(3.38\) micrometres. The fractional frequency shift becomes \(0.675\%\). A third-harmonic signal that instead halves with amplitude could arise from an already distorted input or readout. The two amplitude scalings plus an independent frequency measurement test the cubic model more strongly than observing a line at three times the frequency.

Try it · Duffing harmonic

Vary the physical parameters in the derived relation. Use the units and assumptions in the readout to connect the curves to the two worked examples. A parameter study can test the forward prediction; the same relation can then be inverted to infer a parameter from a measurement.

Open this live calculation

Start from a reversible force law

A spring that looks linear under small deflection can stiffen as it is displaced further. For an oscillator symmetric under \(x\mapsto-x\), the restoring force expanded about equilibrium has no even powers. Keep the leading correction and write \(m\ddot x+kx+\alpha x^3=0\), with \(k>0\) and \(\alpha\) measured in N/m³. Assume the displacement is small enough that neglected fifth-order terms remain unimportant. Positive \(\alpha\) gives a hardening spring. A negative cubic coefficient describes local softening and may need higher-order terms to represent large displacements safely within the model.

The potential is \(kx^2/2+\alpha x^4/4\). Without damping the total energy is conserved and a release at amplitude \(A\) fixes that energy. Unlike a harmonic oscillator, the quadratic curvature at the origin no longer fixes the period for every possible energy. We want a quantitative connection between the amplitude of the motion and its zero-crossing interval.

Obtain the first frequency correction

Try \(x\simeq A\cos\Omega t\) and substitute it into the cubic equation. The identity \(\cos^3 u=(3\cos u+\cos3u)/4\) shows that the nonlinearity introduces a component at the original frequency and a third harmonic. Balance the fundamental coefficient to get \(-m\Omega^2+k+3\alpha A^2/4\simeq0\). Expanding the square root gives

\[\Omega\simeq\omega_0\left(1+\frac{3\alpha A^2}{8k}\right),\]
\[\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}.\]

The control parameter is \(|\alpha|A^2/k\), the ratio of cubic to linear force at maximum displacement. The small additional third harmonic changes the waveform at first order but only feeds back into this leading frequency result at higher order. Fitting a perfect sinusoid to a high-precision trace may therefore show a residual even when the measured average period follows this formula.

Check the result using the conserved energy

The quarter-period is the time to move from equilibrium to \(A\). Substitution of the energy at the turning point gives an integral over \(dx/\sqrt{2[E-U(x)]/m}\). Let \(x=A\sin u\) to remove the square-root endpoint. The remaining integrand is proportional to \(\{1+[\alpha A^2/(2k)](1+\sin^2u)\}^{-1/2}\). Expanding and averaging over the interval from zero to \(\pi/2\) uses mean \(\sin^2 u=1/2\), yielding \(T\simeq(2\pi/\omega_0)[1-3\alpha A^2/(8k)]\). This agrees with the reciprocal of the harmonic-balance result.

The integral approach generalises to experimentally tabulated conservative forces by integrating them first to obtain a potential. It would need modification for strong damping, where energy varies significantly between the two turning points of one cycle.

Infer stiffness from period data

For \(m=0.50\) kg, \(k=200\) N/m and \(\alpha=4.0\times10^4\) N/m³, \(\omega_0=20.0\) rad/s. At \(A=0.020\) m the force ratio is 0.080, giving a leading frequency increase of 3.0% to 20.6 rad/s. At half this amplitude the predicted increase is 0.75%. Measure the period over several cycles at each amplitude, keeping the amplitude change due to loss small. A plot of frequency against the square of amplitude should be approximately straight near the origin. A nonzero intercept shift under a change of temperature could indicate a change in ordinary linear stiffness instead of a new nonlinear coefficient.

Compute the entire amplitude dependence of a pendulum

A cubic expansion is useful near equilibrium. For a pendulum it is possible to carry the energy calculation beyond every finite Taylor approximation. Take a point mass with fixed length \(\ell\), no friction and a release from rest at angle \(0<\theta_0<\pi\). Its conserved energy gives

\[\dot\theta^2=(2g/\ell)(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0).\]

Use \(\cos\theta=1-2\sin^2(\theta/2)\). Defining \(k=\sin(\theta_0/2)\) reduces the speed magnitude to \(2\sqrt{g/\ell}\sqrt{k^2-\sin^2(\theta/2)}\).

One quarter period is the time to travel between zero angle and the turning point. The reciprocal speed appears to diverge at the latter, but it has an integrable square-root singularity for every ordinary turning angle. To evaluate it stably, set \(\sin(\theta/2)=k\sin u\). The factor \(\cos u\) from differentiating cancels the same factor inside the square root. Four equivalent quarters give

\[T=4\sqrt{\ell/g}\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{du}{\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2u}}=4\sqrt{\ell/g}\,K(k).\]

Here \(K\) denotes the complete elliptic integral with modulus \(k\). Expanding the integrand at small \(k\) and integrating the first correction gives

\[T/T_0=1+k^2/4+\cdots=1+\theta_0^2/16+\cdots,\]

where \(T_0=2\pi\sqrt{\ell/g}\). The positive correction is the familiar softening: increasing amplitude lengthens the period because the restoring torque grows more slowly than its linear extrapolation.

Decide when a small-angle clock loses accuracy

A pendulum of length \(0.800\) m has \(T_0=1.794\) s at \(g=9.81\) m/s². At a release of \(60.0^\circ\),

\[k=\sin30^\circ=0.500.\]

Evaluating the integral gives \(K(0.500)=1.68575\) and \(T/T_0=2K/\pi=1.0732\), hence \(T=1.926\) s. The weak-angle approximation gives

\[1+(\pi/3)^2/16=1.0685.\]

It misses the exact period by roughly \(0.008\) s per cycle; a many-cycle timing record resolves the accumulated discrepancy.

As \(\theta_0\) tends to \(\pi\), the integrand near \(u=\pi/2\) approaches the reciprocal of a vanishing cosine. The integral diverges logarithmically, expressing the long time spent close to the unstable upper equilibrium. No finite polynomial in amplitude can reproduce that divergence. A numerical timing experiment should therefore locate regular zero crossings rather than demand a turning-point velocity of exactly zero in sampled data. Comparing the crossing intervals with the regularized integral distinguishes numerical resolution error from the genuine increase in physical period.

A way to evaluate the elliptic integral without a special-function library is to form the arithmetic–geometric mean. Begin with \(a_0=1\) and \(b_0=\sqrt{1-k^2}\), then replace the pair by their arithmetic and geometric means. Both converge rapidly to a common \(M\), and \(K(k)=\pi/(2M)\). For the 60° release the first pair is \(1\) and \(0.86603\), the next pair is approximately \(0.93301\) and \(0.93060\), and the subsequent pair agrees near \(0.93181\). Taking the reciprocal of the common value directly gives the period ratio. This procedure supplies an accurate independent benchmark even when the small-amplitude expansion ceases to converge quickly.

Numerical quadrature and the arithmetic–geometric mean should agree at a fixed amplitude. If a period extracted from actual trajectories differs while these two evaluations agree, examine the dynamical time step, how release angle is measured, and whether the observed oscillations have suffered appreciable damping.

Chapter 12 · Bifurcation of a rotating hoop

Use an effective potential to locate competing equilibria and predict the frequency of small oscillations on either side of a stability change.

From first principles

Find the instability threshold of the rotating hoop

Assume a frictionless bead constrained to a vertical circular hoop of radius \(R\). The hoop rotates at prescribed constant angular speed \(\Omega\) about its vertical diameter. With angle \(\theta\) measured upward from the bottom, the bead moves along the hoop at speed \(R\dot\theta\) and around the axis at speed \(\Omega R\sin\theta\). These directions are perpendicular, and its gravitational height above the bottom is \(R(1-\cos\theta)\). Thus its Lagrangian is

\[L=\tfrac12mR^2(\dot\theta^2+\Omega^2\sin^2\theta)-mgR(1-\cos\theta).\]

Apply the one-coordinate Lagrange equation. The rotation term tends to move the bead outward while gravity acts toward the bottom:

\[\ddot\theta=\sin\theta(\Omega^2\cos\theta-g/R).\]

Linearizing about the bottom gives

\[\ddot\theta\simeq(\Omega^2-g/R)\theta.\]

For \(\Omega^2<g/R\) the coefficient restores a small displacement; above threshold the bottom has growing small disturbances. Setting the exact right side to zero gives the additional equilibrium and its range:

\[\Omega_c=\sqrt{g/R},\]
\[\cos\theta_*=g/(R\Omega^2)\quad(\Omega\ge\Omega_c).\]

The two nonzero angles are related by reflection. Their existence follows from the prescribed rotation, so a freely slowing hoop would require an additional dynamical coordinate.

Derivation and applications

How high is the barrier between the two tilted equilibria?

In the rotating hoop, a new pair of stable angles appears where the bottom loses stability. Its curvature predicts a small-oscillation frequency; its depth determines whether a larger disturbance can carry the bead across the bottom. Consider a bead of mass \(m\) on a circular hoop of radius \(R\) spinning at prescribed constant angular speed \(\Omega\) about its vertical diameter. Ignore friction. Measure \(\theta\) upward along the hoop from the bottom. The vertical height change is \(R(1-\cos\theta)\) and the distance to the rotation axis is \(R\sin\theta\).

The constrained bead has kinetic energy \(mR^2(\dot\theta^2+\Omega^2\sin^2\theta)/2\). Collect the terms independent of \(\dot\theta\) as the potential governing motion in the rotating coordinate:

\[U_{\rm eff}(\theta)=mgR(1-\cos\theta)-\tfrac12mR^2\Omega^2\sin^2\theta .\]

Write \(s=\Omega^2R/g\) and differentiate. A tilted equilibrium exists only for \(s>1\). At either stable angle \(\theta_*\) substitute \(\cos\theta_*=1/s\) into the potential and factor the result:

\[U'_{\rm eff}=mgR\sin\theta(1-s\cos\theta),\]
\[U_{\rm eff}(\theta_*)=-mgR\,\frac{(s-1)^2}{2s}.\]

The bottom has \(U_{\rm eff}(0)=0\). Subtracting the energies gives the barrier and the threshold angular speed for a bead launched from a tilted minimum toward the bottom:

\[\Delta U=mgR\,\frac{(s-1)^2}{2s},\]
\[|\dot\theta|_{\rm th}=\sqrt{2\Delta U/(mR^2)}.\]

The velocity here is angular speed relative to the hoop. At threshold the trajectory approaches the unstable bottom asymptotically; crossing takes slightly more initial energy. Near \(s=1\) the barrier collapses quadratically even though two distinct equilibria already exist. The externally maintained rotation can exchange ordinary laboratory energy with the bead, while the effective one-coordinate energy is conserved.

Worked example

Estimate the speed needed to change branches

Change the inputs and investigate this derivation.

Take \(m=0.0500\) kg, \(R=0.200\) m and choose \(\Omega\) so that \(s=2.00\). The two minima then occur at \(\pm60.0^\circ\) and the barrier is

\[mgR/4=0.0245\,\mathrm{J}.\]

The tangential threshold speed is \(\sqrt{2\Delta U/m}=0.990\) m/s, or \(4.95\) rad/s along the hoop. A launch at \(0.800\) m/s has only \(0.0160\) J and returns to its original branch.

Second application

Use two measured angles to compare barrier depths

Change the inputs and investigate this derivation.

On the same hoop reduce the rotation until the two minima are at \(\pm36.9^\circ\). Their cosine is about \(0.800\), giving \(s=1.25\). The new barrier is \(mgR(0.25)^2/2.50=0.00245\) J, a tenth of the previous value. The new threshold tangential speed is \(0.313\) m/s. A smaller change in angle than this tenfold energy reduction might suggest is a measurable feature of a shallow double well.

Locate the bifurcation by measuring curvature

A vertical hoop rotates about its vertical diameter at a prescribed angular speed \(\Omega\). A frictionless bead can move along the hoop. Measure \(\theta\) from the bottom. The laboratory kinetic energy is \(mR^2(\dot\theta^2+\Omega^2\sin^2\theta)/2\). In the equation for the bead the effective potential per unit \(mgR\) is \(-\cos\theta-(\Omega^2R/2g)\sin^2\theta\). Its derivative factors as \(\sin\theta[1-(\Omega^2R/g)\cos\theta]\).

Open this experiment online

Plot the potential before and after crossing \(\Omega_c=\sqrt{g/R}\). At a stable equilibrium the slope vanishes and the curvature is positive. Above the critical speed the bottom loses positive curvature and two stable angles appear. The motor holding \(\Omega\) fixed exchanges angular momentum with the system. A freely rotating hoop with fixed total angular momentum describes a different experiment.

Reduce the constraint to one coordinate

A bead slides on a vertical circular hoop of radius \(R\). An external motor rotates the hoop at prescribed constant angular velocity \(\Omega\) about its vertical diameter. Let \(\theta\) be the angle from the lowest point. The bead’s height relative to that point is \(R(1-\cos\theta)\) and its distance from the rotation axis is \(R\sin\theta\). Assume negligible friction and a rigid constraint. The bead moves both along the hoop and azimuthally with it, even if \(\theta\) is momentarily stationary.

In laboratory coordinates its speed squared is \(R^2\dot\theta^2+\Omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta\). Subtract gravitational potential energy from this kinetic energy to construct a one-coordinate Lagrangian. Lagrange’s equation gives

\[\ddot\theta=\sin\theta(\Omega^2\cos\theta-g/R).\]

Although motion in the laboratory is constrained by a driven apparatus, the reduced equation is autonomous for constant \(\Omega\).

Track equilibria as the rotation rate changes

The torque vanishes at the bottom and the top because \(\sin\theta=0\). Off-axis equilibria also appear when \(\cos\theta=g/(\Omega^2R)\). They are possible only if the rotation exceeds \(\Omega_c=\sqrt{g/R}\). Each positive-angle equilibrium then has a negative-angle partner. The two have equal energies because the apparatus is symmetric.

For small displacement from the bottom,

\[\ddot\theta\simeq-(g/R-\Omega^2)\theta.\]

Below threshold the bottom is stable with angular frequency \(\sqrt{g/R-\Omega^2}\). As the threshold is approached this frequency tends to zero; the potential flattens. Above threshold the sign reverses and a small perturbation grows. Linearising about either displaced equilibrium instead gives a positive frequency squared \(\Omega^2\sin^2\theta_{\rm eq}\). Measuring this small-amplitude response distinguishes two predictions: where the bead rests and how steeply it is restored when disturbed.

Interpret the effective energy

The reduced motion admits the effective potential \(U_{\rm eff}=mgR(1-\cos\theta)-m\Omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta/2\). Its derivative predicts the reduced equation. Its negative centrifugal term differs in sign from the positive laboratory azimuthal kinetic energy. The motor supplies or absorbs work as the bead’s distance from the rotation axis changes. Treating the bead’s laboratory mechanical energy alone as conserved would therefore lead to the wrong equilibrium.

At exactly the critical rate, the quadratic terms in a small-angle expansion cancel and the first restoring term in \(U_{\rm eff}\) is positive and quartic. A finite disturbance can still oscillate there, but its period depends on its amplitude. An arbitrarily small oscillation cannot be assigned a finite harmonic frequency at that point.

Estimate the transition in a real apparatus

With \(R=0.250\) m and \(g=9.81\) m/s² the critical rate is 6.26 rad/s, or about 59.8 rpm. At 5.0 rad/s the bead returns to the bottom with small-oscillation frequency \(\sqrt{39.24-25}=3.77\) rad/s. At 8.0 rad/s the two new equilibria satisfy \(\cos\theta=39.24/64=0.613\), or \(\theta=\pm52.2°\). Small oscillations about either have angular frequency \(8\sqrt{1-0.613^2}=6.32\) rad/s.

When observing the transition, tilt of the axis or a small asymmetry of the hoop can favour one side. Hysteresis-like delays during a fast sweep can also arise from finite settling time in weak damping. Recording both equilibrium angles on slow sweeps and the independently measured oscillation frequency supplies a more discriminating test of the symmetric bifurcation than simply noting which side the bead occupies.

Break the symmetry with a weak bias

The two off-centre positions of the ideal rotating bead have equal energy. A small constant generalized torque \(\tau_b\) favouring positive \(\theta\) breaks that symmetry. Over a small working angular range it adds a term \(-\tau_b\theta\) to the effective potential. Write the original potential relative to its value at the bottom as \(mgR(1-\cos\theta)-m\Omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta/2\). Expanding near the critical rate \(\Omega_c^2=g/R\) gives quadratic coefficient \(mR^2(\Omega_c^2-\Omega^2)/2\). The quartic coefficient evaluated at threshold is \(mR^2\Omega_c^2/8\).

On the high-speed side define \(a=\Omega^2-\Omega_c^2>0\), \(b=\Omega_c^2/2\), and \(h=\tau_b/(mR^2)\). To leading order stationarity and local stability become

\[b\theta^3-a\theta-h=0,\qquad 3b\theta^2-a>0 .\]

With zero bias there are two symmetric minima and an unstable central position. Increasing positive bias deepens the positive minimum and eventually destroys the negative one. At the point where the negative minimum meets the adjacent maximum, both the stationarity equation and its derivative in \(\theta\) vanish. Thus

\[\theta_*=-\sqrt{a/(3b)},\]
\[h_*=(2a/3)\sqrt{a/(3b)}.\]

The critical bias scales as \(a^{3/2}\). Near the threshold a surprisingly small imperfection can remove one of the two resting positions entirely.

Estimate the bias needed to select a branch

Use a bead of mass \(0.0500\) kg on a hoop of radius \(0.250\) m. Then \(\Omega_c^2=39.24\) s⁻². Set \(\Omega^2=\Omega_c^2+0.600\) s⁻², making \(b=19.62\) s⁻². The unbiased displaced equilibrium angles are approximately \(\pm\sqrt{0.600/19.62}=\pm0.175\) rad. As positive bias is increased, the negative branch disappears near \(\theta_*=-0.101\) rad. The corresponding generalized acceleration is \(h_*=0.0404\) s⁻², giving \(\tau_b=mR^2h_*=1.26\times10^{-4}\) N m. A tangential force with moment arm \(R\) would supply about \(0.505\) mN.

This estimate uses both small angles and operation close enough to the critical speed that quartic truncation is accurate. An exact calculation differentiates the full trigonometric potential twice and solves the two equations simultaneously. In a slow sweep with weak damping, a bead initially on the unfavoured branch can remain there until its minimum disappears. Vibration or thermal agitation may make it switch earlier by crossing the remaining barrier. Repeating the sweep in both directions and at several bias amplitudes helps distinguish an imperfect constraint from random switching in a nearly symmetric system.

The same model predicts increasing sensitivity before an actual switch. Differentiate the cubic stationarity condition with respect to bias while following a particular equilibrium branch:

\[d\theta/dh=1/(3b\theta^2-a).\]

Its denominator is the local dimensionless restoring curvature. Thus a branch nearing disappearance both moves a large angular distance under a small bias increment and shows a very low small-oscillation frequency. Measuring those two effects on the same branch tests the local shape of the potential without requiring a precise measurement of the noisy switching moment. Away from a minimum the static slope can instead be negative, describing an unstable mathematical solution.

The sharp loss of a branch is best resolved with bias steps small compared with the measured interval between its creation and disappearance.

Where will a bead settle on a rotating hoop?

Choose zero potential at the bottom. Gravity contributes \(mgR(1-\cos\theta)\); the rotating-frame centrifugal term contributes \(-m\Omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta/2\). Inspect both the slope and the curvature at the bottom while increasing speed.

Problem sheet 6 · Nonlinear frequencies and broken symmetry

Identify nonlinear stiffness and track equilibria as a rotating constraint changes stability.

Fit a weak cubic spring

A mass of 0.20 kg has a natural frequency of 10.00 Hz at negligible amplitude. At 10.0 mm amplitude it oscillates at 10.03 Hz. Assume a restoring force \(-kx-\beta x^3\). Estimate \(k\) and \(\beta\), predict the shift at 5.0 mm and test the perturbation assumption.

Show the stiffness estimates

The linear coefficient is

\[k=m(2\pi f_0)^2=790\,\mathrm{N/m}.\]

Retaining the fundamental of \(\cos^3\omega t\) gives \(\Delta f/f_0\simeq3\beta A^2/(8k)\). Hence \(\beta=8k(0.0030)/(3\times10^{-4})=6.32\times10^4\) N/m³. The positive sign describes hardening. At half amplitude the shift falls by four, to \(0.0075\) Hz. The maximum cubic-to-linear force ratio at 10 mm is \(\beta A^2/k=0.0080\), compatible with a first-order estimate.

Which equilibria can hold a bead?

A bead slides without friction on a vertical hoop of radius 0.400 m rotating about its vertical diameter. Find the critical angular speed and stable positions at 6.00 rad/s. Determine the small oscillation frequency about either tilted position and compare with operation at 4.00 rad/s.

Show the stability calculation

With angle measured from the bottom the effective potential per unit mass is \(-gR\cos\theta-\Omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta/2\). Its derivative is \(R\sin\theta(g-\Omega^2R\cos\theta)\). The critical speed is

\[\sqrt{g/R}=4.95\,\mathrm{rad/s}.\]

At 6.00 rad/s the tilted minima have \(\cos\theta=9.81/(36\times0.4)=0.6813\), hence \(\theta=\pm47.1^\circ\). Curvature divided by \(R^2\) gives \(\omega^2=\Omega^2\sin^2\theta\), or \(\omega=4.39\) rad/s. At 4.00 rad/s only the bottom is stable and \(\omega=\sqrt{g/R-\Omega^2}=2.92\) rad/s.

Tilt a symmetric double well

For dimensionless displacement \(x\), a potential is \(V/E_0=x^4/4-ax^2/2-hx\) with \(a=0.12\). Find equilibria and barrier height at \(h=0\). Determine the magnitude of bias where one metastable well disappears and explain why the transition can depend on sweep history.

Show the barrier and the loss of stability

At zero bias stationary points solve \(x(x^2-a)=0\). Curvature \(3x^2-a\) gives minima at \(\pm\sqrt{a}=\pm0.346\) and a maximum at zero. The energy barrier is

\[a^2E_0/4=0.00360E_0.\]

A minimum and adjacent maximum merge when \(3x^2=a\) and \(h=x^3-ax\). Thus

\[|h|=2(a/3)^{3/2}=0.0160.\]

A weakly damped or cold system initially captured in the unfavoured well can remain there as the bias crosses zero. In a slowly driven, damped experiment without appreciable fluctuations it switches near the disappearance of that minimum; noise can trigger earlier switching.

Reconstruct a binary orbit from a spectrum

Two spectral lines trace a circular binary with a period of 20.0 days. Their radial-velocity semi-amplitudes are 30.0 and 60.0 km/s. Take the orbit to be edge-on. Find the stellar separation, both masses and the orbital energy. How would the mass estimate change at an inclination of 60°? Use G = 6.6743 × 10⁻¹¹ in SI units and one solar mass = 1.9885 × 10³⁰ kg.

Worked solution

The two stars orbit their common centre of mass with the same angular frequency. Their speeds add to give a relative circular speed of 90,000 m/s. Over 1,728,000 s the relative separation vector describes a circle of circumference 2πa, hence a = 2.475 × 10¹⁰ m. The speed ratio gives the inverse mass ratio. The star moving at 30 km/s is twice as massive as the other star.

The relative acceleration is v²/a and the two-body attraction gives G(M₁+M₂)/a². Equating the expressions gives 3.00 × 10³⁰ kg in total, about 1.51 solar masses. The individual masses are approximately 1.01 and 0.50 solar masses. The reduced mass is two ninths of the total. Its kinetic energy is ½μv², and the total orbital energy is its negative, approximately −2.70 × 10³⁹ J.

If the inclination falls to 60°, the observed speeds are projections of the larger orbital speeds. The separation scales as 1/sin i, and the inferred mass as 1/sin³ i. The total rises by a factor of 1.54. Spectroscopy alone fixes the mass ratio and a projected mass. An independent inclination from an eclipse or astrometric orbit breaks the degeneracy.

Chapter 13 · Changing the coordinates of a moving trap

A translating trap looks stationary in its own coordinates. Derive the Hamiltonian measured by that observer, including the term that accounts for motion of the coordinate system.

What does a change of coordinates have to preserve?

A counter moving along a rail reports the bead position relative to the counter. Its reading alone does not transform the bead momentum or tell us how energy changes in the moving frame. Let the laboratory Hamiltonian be \(H(q,p,t)\). The phase-space action integrates \(p\dot q-H\) between specified configurations. Adding a total time derivative changes that integral only at the ends. It therefore provides a way to construct new coordinates in which the same interior trajectories make the action stationary.

Demand that the old and new action forms differ by an exact differential. A convenient function uses the old position and the new momentum as arguments. Subtract \(QP\) from it to convert the independent end variables. The product rule gives

\[p\,dq-H\,dt=P\,dQ-K\,dt+d(F_2-QP)=dF_2-Q\,dP-K\,dt .\]

Now compare the coefficients of the independent differentials separately. The new energy has an extra term whenever the coordinate map depends explicitly on time.

\[p=\partial_q F_2,\]
\[Q=\partial_P F_2,\]
\[K=H+\partial_t F_2 .\]

For a simple test take \(F_2=\lambda qP\) with constant positive \(\lambda\). Then \(Q=\lambda q\) and \(P=p/\lambda\). A position interval stretches while the conjugate momentum interval shrinks by the reciprocal factor. The product \(dq\,dp\) stays fixed. This checks the derivative rules without using a particular force law.

Move the origin and then move the momentum

Take the trap centre to be \(a(t)\) and the laboratory potential to be \(k(q-a)^2/2\). Choosing \(F_2=(q-a)P\) gives

\[Q=q-a,\ p=P.\]

Thus the coordinate is relative position, but its conjugate momentum still equals the laboratory momentum. Hamilton's velocity equation reads \(\dot Q=P/m-\dot a\), exactly the velocity seen by the moving counter.

To obtain a momentum equal to \(m\dot Q\), choose \(F_2=(q-a)(P+m\dot a)+g(t)\). This produces \(p=P+m\dot a\). Substitute it into the kinetic energy and the explicit time derivative of the generator. The cross terms \(\dot a P\) cancel. The remaining terms depending on time alone can be removed by choosing \(\dot g=m\dot a^2/2\). The result is

\[K=\frac{P^2}{2m}+\frac{kQ^2}{2}+m\ddot a\,Q,\]
\[m\ddot Q=-kQ-m\ddot a .\]

The apparent force comes from the acceleration of the reference point. A constant translation speed drops out of this final equation. A time-dependent acceleration can do work on the relative motion, so the bead's relative mechanical energy need not be conserved.

Predict a displaced equilibrium

Use a 0.50 kg bead and a spring with \(k=8.0\) N/m. Accelerate the support uniformly at \(1.6\) m/s² in the positive direction. A stationary bead in the accelerating frame has \(Q_*=-m\ddot a/k=-0.100\) m. Relative oscillations about this new centre have the original angular frequency \(4.0\) rad/s. The curvature of the potential sets the frequency and the added linear term changes its minimum.

If the bead is initially at \(Q=0\) with zero relative velocity when acceleration starts, its subsequent displacement is

\[Q=Q_*[1-\cos(\omega t)].\]

At \(t=\pi/\omega=0.7854\) s it reaches \(-0.200\) m, twice the static shift. It then returns. An overdamped measuring device would instead approach the static reading without that overshoot. Damping has been omitted here.

Set the support acceleration

Predict the sign of the first turning point when the acceleration reverses. Change the acceleration, then change the spring stiffness. Track separately the position of the equilibrium and the time between successive extrema.

Open this experiment online

Tutorial on reconstructing the motion

A bead released from the old equilibrium reaches its first relative extremum at −0.060 m after 0.50 s. Find its angular frequency and the support acceleration.

Work through the solution

The first extremum occurs after half a cycle, giving \(\omega=\pi/0.50=6.283\) rad/s. The equilibrium shift is half the extremum, \(Q_*=-0.030\) m. The equation for that shift gives

\[\ddot a=-\omega^2Q_*=1.18\,\mathrm{m/s^2}.\]

Both quantities follow from the trajectory without a separate mass measurement.

Check the momentum transformation directly by measuring kinetic energy. In a frame attached to a support moving at constant \(0.30\,\mathrm{m/s}\), a \(0.50\) kg bead has \(P=0.20\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}\) along the support velocity. What laboratory momentum and kinetic energy should an observer assign?

Work through the solution

The moving-frame kinetic momentum is \(m(\dot q-\dot a)\). Thus \(p=P+m\dot a=0.35\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}\), the relative kinetic energy is \(P^2/(2m)=0.0400\,\mathrm J\) and the laboratory kinetic energy is

\[p^2/(2m)=0.1225\,\mathrm J.\]

Expanding the square gives the missing cross term \(P\dot a=0.0600\,\mathrm J\) and offset \(m\dot a^2/2=0.0225\,\mathrm J\).

A support acceleration varies with time. How could you reconstruct it from a measured relative trajectory, and which measurements become unreliable first in the presence of position noise?

Work through the solution

Rearranging the equation gives

\[\ddot a=-\ddot Q-kQ/m.\]

A static deflection measures only constant acceleration after transients are controlled. In a time-dependent experiment a second time derivative is unavoidable for this inversion. It amplifies short-time position noise, so fitted trajectories or independent acceleration data can test the reconstruction.

Further reading · Fließbach, Mechanik, Hamiltonformalismus · Tong, Classical Dynamics, canonical transformations.

Study the full derivation

Noether's theorem, boundary terms and measurable constants · Analytical mechanics from constraints to invariants

A constant of motion can survive when neither laboratory energy nor angular momentum is separately conserved. Construct the conserved quantity from an infinitesimal transformation of the action. Then use boosts, a screw symmetry, and a rotating potential to determine what measured combinations should stay fixed.

Chapter 14 · Recover a trajectory from a family of actions

In Hamilton–Jacobi theory a partial differential equation for one function replaces several trajectory equations. A falling bead makes the different roles of position, energy and arrival time explicit.

Use the end of the path as a variable

Let a bead move between a fixed initial event and an adjustable final event. Denote by \(S(q,t)\) the action evaluated on the actual trajectory ending at \((q,t)\). For a small change in the endpoint, the interior variation cancels by the Euler–Lagrange equation. If time stays fixed the boundary term is \(p\,\delta q\). If time changes, part of the endpoint displacement comes from continuing along the existing path by \(\dot q\,\delta t\). The remaining independent displacement is \(\delta q-\dot q\,\delta t\). Thus

\[\delta S=p(\delta q-\dot q\,\delta t)+L\,\delta t=p\,\delta q-H\,\delta t .\]

It follows that \(p=\partial_q S\) and \(-H=\partial_t S\). Eliminate \(p\) to obtain

\[\partial_t S+H(q,\partial_q S,t)=0 .\]

The equation involves partial derivatives because it describes an entire family of possible endpoints. By contrast, \(dS/dt=L\) along a single trajectory. A useful dimensional check is that a derivative of action with respect to length is momentum, whereas a derivative with respect to time is energy.

Separate time and build a clock from energy

For a time-independent Hamiltonian try \(S=W(q;E)-Et\). With \(H=p^2/(2m)+U(q)\), this gives

\[(\partial_qW)^2=2m(E-U).\]

A trajectory on the increasing-position branch has positive momentum, so an integral from a fixed reference position \(q_0\) supplies \(W\). Differentiate at fixed final position with respect to the family parameter \(E\):

\[W=\int_{q_0}^{q}\!\sqrt{2m(E-U(s))}\,ds,\]
\[\partial_EW=\int_{q_0}^{q}\!\frac{m\,ds}{\sqrt{2m(E-U(s))}} .\]

The integrand of the second integral is \(1/v\). Hence \(\partial_E W\) is the travel time from the reference point. Setting \(\partial_E S=0\) chooses a departure time of zero with this lower integration limit. A different constant amounts to shifting the clock. At a turning point \(p=0\), the one-way branch must be changed to continue the motion.

Work two arrival-time problems

Let \(q=x\) point downwards, \(U=-mgx\), and release the bead through \(x=0\) with speed \(u\). Its energy is

\[E=mu^2/2.\]

The integral yields

\[t=(\sqrt{u^2+2gx}-u)/g.\]

Squaring the relation after isolating the square root gives \(x=ut+gt^2/2\), the same trajectory as Newton's equation. For \(u=2.0\) m/s, \(g=9.81\) m/s² and \(x=3.0\) m the arrival time is about \(0.604\) s. The endpoint momentum uses the final speed, about \(7.93\) m/s, rather than the average over the fall.

Reverse the experiment by pointing \(x\) upward in the same field. If \(u=4.0\) m/s, the maximum height is \(0.815\) m. A gate \(0.50\) m above launch is crossed twice. From \(x=ut-gt^2/2\) the two times are \(0.154\) s and \(0.661\) s. The need for two branches of \(W\) is experimentally visible in those two timestamps. A calculation that takes the positive square root everywhere loses the return journey.

Compare two launch speeds

The plot shows upward trajectories and their common observation height. Lower the launch speed towards the value that barely reaches the gate. Watch what happens to the separation between the two arrival times.

Open this experiment online

Tutorial on the double root

A gate records two crossings 0.40 s apart in a uniform field of 9.81 m/s². How high does the trajectory rise above that gate?

Work through the solution

The two crossings are symmetric about the maximum. The fall from the maximum takes 0.20 s, giving \(g(0.20)^2/2=0.1962\) m. Equivalently the speed at the gate is \(g(0.40)/2=1.962\) m/s and its kinetic energy per unit mass gives the same height.

Estimate the arrival-time sensitivity of a gate on the rising branch. At \(u=4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}\) compare \(h=0.50\) m with \(h=0.80\) m.

Work through the solution

Implicit differentiation of \(h=ut-gt^2/2\) at fixed launch speed gives

\[dt/dh=1/(u-gt).\]

On ascent this is \(1/\sqrt{u^2-2gh}\). Its value grows from \(0.402\,\mathrm{s/m}\) at 0.50 m to \(1.81\,\mathrm{s/m}\) at 0.80 m. Close to the top a small height error produces much larger timing uncertainty because the trajectory crosses slowly.

Does adding a constant \(C\) to a potential alter the predicted arrival times from Hamilton–Jacobi theory when the initial position and speed are unchanged?

Work through the solution

Both the total energy label and potential shift by \(C\). Hence \(p=\sqrt{2m(E-U)}\) and the abbreviated action as a path integral of \(p\) are unchanged for that orbit. The full action acquires \(-Ct\). Its spatial derivative and the time crossing predictions remain the same. Comparing the same numerical energy before and after the shift would specify different trajectories.

Further reading · Fließbach, Hamiltonformalismus · Tong, Hamilton–Jacobi theory.

Study the full derivation

Two phase-space plots can enclose the same volume while predicting different responses to an impulse. Derive the stronger condition that makes a change of variables canonical, test it on measured linear maps and use Poisson brackets to propagate observables without solving separately for every coordinate.

Chapter 15 · Read a period from the area enclosed by an orbit

A track with a V-shaped potential has straight force segments but a strongly amplitude-dependent period. Its area in phase space gives a useful way to predict both the period and a slow change of the track.

Construct the closed area

For one bound degree of freedom at energy \(E\), position runs between two turning points. In a mechanical Hamiltonian \(p^2/(2m)+U(q)\), the upper branch of the phase portrait has positive momentum and the lower branch has its negative. The directed integral around one full orbit counts the enclosed area. Define the action \(J\) using the area divided by \(2\pi\). This choice makes its conjugate phase an angle measured in radians:

\[J(E)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\oint p\,dq=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{q_-}^{q_+}\sqrt{2m(E-U(q))}\,dq .\]

Now change the energy slightly. The integrand vanishes at each regular endpoint, so the moving-endpoint contributions to the derivative vanish. In the interior \(\partial p/\partial E=m/p=1/v\). The derivative of the upper-branch area therefore measures the time to reach the opposite turning point.

\[\frac{dJ}{dE}=\frac{T(E)}{2\pi},\]
\[\omega(E)=\frac{dE}{dJ}.\]

This argument also explains why the construction becomes delicate near a separatrix. A trajectory can spend an arbitrarily long time near an unstable equilibrium, and \(T\) can diverge even though the enclosed area stays finite.

Background · Action variable
\[J=(2\pi)^{-1}\oint p\,dq\]

This area measure is defined for a closed cycle. It can change strongly near a separatrix even under a slow parameter variation.

Carry out the integral for a constant restoring force

Use \(U(q)=F|q|\) with \(F>0\). The turning amplitude is \(A=E/F\). Integrate the positive branch from \(0\) to \(A\) and use reflection symmetry. Substitution \(s=E-Fq\) gives

\[J=\frac{4\sqrt{2m}}{3\pi F}E^{3/2},\]
\[T=\frac{4\sqrt{2mE}}{F}=4\sqrt{\frac{2mA}{F}} .\]

The answer has an independent mechanical check. From a turning point the bead accelerates uniformly with magnitude \(F/m\) until the centre. Covering a distance \(A\) from rest takes \(\sqrt{2mA/F}\), a quarter period. Doubling the amplitude increases the full period by \(\sqrt{2}\). The abrupt change of force direction at the centre leaves the velocity continuous.

Slowly steepen the track

A slowly adjusted parameter can preserve the orbit action to leading order when the motion remains periodic and many cycles fit inside the adjustment time. For this trap \(m\) stays constant, so constant \(J\) requires \(E^{3/2}/F\) to stay fixed. Therefore \(E\propto F^{2/3}\),

\[A=E/F\propto F^{-1/3},\]
\[T\propto F^{-2/3}.\]

Work done by adjusting the slope changes the energy despite the approximate conservation of action.

Start with \(m=0.25\) kg, \(F=2.0\) N and \(A=0.080\) m. The initial energy is \(0.160\) J and the period \(0.566\) s. A slow eightfold increase of \(F\) makes the energy four times larger, \(0.640\) J, and the amplitude half as large, \(0.040\) m. The period becomes \(0.141\) s. In contrast, switching slopes instantaneously at the centre leaves the kinetic energy and position unchanged at that instant. The same final slope would then give amplitude \(0.010\) m. The route by which a parameter changes matters.

Compare closed orbits at constant action

The axes are position and momentum. Change the slope ratio. Predict how the turning positions and the central momentum move in opposite directions. Their changes balance in the enclosed area.

Open this experiment online

Tutorial on inferring a change

After a slow adjustment the period is 64% of its original value. Find the force and amplitude ratios.

Work through the solution

From \(T_f/T_i=(F_f/F_i)^{-2/3}\), the force ratio is

\[0.64^{-3/2}=1.953125.\]

The amplitude ratio is its inverse cube root, \(0.800\). Squaring the period formula with these values provides an independent check.

Derive a relation between the area action and the product of energy and period in the V trap. What fraction of the total energy is kinetic on a time average over one orbit?

Work through the solution

The explicit formulas give \(J=ET/(3\pi)\), a quantity with units of action. Along the orbit \(p\,dq=p\dot q\,dt=2K\,dt\). Hence \(2\pi J=2T\langle K\rangle\) and \(\langle K\rangle=E/3\), leaving \(2E/3\) in potential energy. This is an independent check using a measurable time average.

A trap is weakened gradually until the amplitude doubles. Find the predicted changes in energy and period, and state when the slow-ramp argument is most vulnerable.

Work through the solution

The amplitude varies as \(F^{-1/3}\), so doubling it requires reducing \(F\) to one eighth. The energy then falls to one quarter and the period increases fourfold. A ramp duration adequate initially can become too short compared to the final period. Checking the endpoint period alone is insufficient if the control has sharp changes during the ramp.

Further reading · Tong, action–angle coordinates and adiabatic invariants.

A phase portrait contains enough information to extract a period by differentiating an area. Use that fact to build a clock for finite-amplitude pendulum motion, determine precisely where slow-parameter invariance fails, and distinguish a librating trajectory from one that makes complete rotations.

Chapter 16 · From a chain of springs to an elastic field

A rod ringing after a small axial displacement can be described by one differential equation at every point. Derive that field equation, its boundary conditions and the range of wavelengths for which it represents a discrete chain.

Take a limit that represents the same rod

Divide a rod of cross-sectional area \(A\), mass density \(\rho\), length \(L\) and Young modulus \(Y\) into segments of length \(a\). Let \(u_j(t)\) be the axial displacement at a site. Each segment carries mass \(\rho Aa\). Under a small relative displacement \(\Delta u\) the strain is \(\Delta u/a\). Hooke's law gives force \(YA\Delta u/a\), hence the segment spring constant is \(YA/a\). Refining the chain must change both its masses and its springs by these rules to preserve the material.

\[\rho Aa\,\ddot u_j=\frac{YA}{a}(u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}).\]

For a smooth displacement the second difference is \(a^2u_{xx}+a^4u_{xxxx}/12+\cdots\). Cancel a common factor of \(Aa\). The leading continuum equation is \(\rho u_{tt}=Yu_{xx}\) with wave speed \(c=\sqrt{Y/\rho}\). The next term already shows why sharp disturbances with wavelengths close to \(a\) require the discrete chain.

Vary the field and keep the endpoint term

Alternatively add the kinetic and elastic energy densities using \(u_x\) for strain. The action per unit length integrated over time is

\[S=\int dt\int_0^L dx\,\left(\frac{\rho A}{2}u_t^2-\frac{YA}{2}u_x^2\right).\]

Vary \(u\) by any smooth small displacement that vanishes at the initial and final times. Integrating its time derivative by parts returns \(-\rho A u_{tt}\). Integrating the space derivative by parts returns \(+\partial_x(YA u_x)\) together with an endpoint term \(-[YA u_x\,\delta u]_0^L\). The interior coefficient must vanish independently. A clamped end fixes \(\delta u=0\) there. A free end permits arbitrary virtual displacement and thus requires zero axial traction \(YA u_x=0\). An externally applied force would contribute boundary work to the action. This reasoning keeps the correct equation even when stiffness and cross section vary with position.

Measure the first resonance

For a uniform rod clamped at zero, \(u=X(x)\cos(\omega t)\) gives

\[X=C\sin(kx),\]

with \(\omega=ck\). A free end at \(L\) requires \(\cos(kL)=0\), so \(k_n=(n+1/2)\pi/L\). With \(L=0.80\) m, \(Y=70.0\) GPa and \(\rho=2700\) kg/m³, \(c=5092\) m/s and the first axial resonance is

\[c/(4L)=1591\,\mathrm{Hz}.\]

Clamping both ends requires \(X(L)=0\), changing that first frequency to 3183 Hz. The material has stayed the same while the measured spectrum has changed.

For the infinite chain substitute \(u_j=e^{i(kja-\omega t)}\) directly into the second difference. The factors sum to \(2\cos(ka)-2=-4\sin^2(ka/2)\). Hence \(\omega=2c|\sin(ka/2)|/a\). At \(ka=\pi/2\) the ratio to the continuum frequency is

\[2\sqrt2/\pi=0.9003.\]

Shorter wavelength changes the phase advance between neighbouring sites more strongly, making the smooth-gradient approximation less accurate.

Test wavelength resolution

Change the number of sites per wavelength and read the discrete frequency relative to the continuum prediction. Compare the phase speed with the group speed \(d\omega/dk\), which controls a narrow packet of modes.

Open this experiment online

Tutorial on the continuum error

A mesh has ten sites per wavelength. Estimate its fractional phase-speed error first by series expansion, then with the sine formula.

Work through the solution

With \(x=ka/2=\pi/10\), the ratio is \(\sin x/x\). Keeping \(1-x^2/6\) predicts a deficit of 0.01645. Direct evaluation gives 0.01637, about 1.64%. Doubling the sites per wavelength reduces the leading error by a factor of four.

A frequency scan of the same rod finds equally spaced resonances from 1.59 kHz onwards at 3.18 kHz intervals. Predict the axial displacement at the support and the stress at the opposite end. Which observation distinguishes a clamped–free from a free–free rod?

Work through the solution

The sequence \(f_n=(2n+1)c/(4L)\) agrees with the clamped–free case. At the clamp displacement vanishes, while at the opposite end the axial derivative and therefore stress vanish. A free–free rod also has zero stress at both ends, but its nonzero resonances are integer multiples of \(c/(2L)\); it also permits a zero-frequency rigid translation.

For a narrow wave packet at four sites per central wavelength, use the dispersion relation to compare the arrival of the centre of the packet with a single crest.

Work through the solution

Here \(ka/2=\pi/4\). The phase travels at \(c\sin(\pi/4)/(\pi/4)=0.9003c\), whereas the envelope moves at \(c\cos(\pi/4)=0.7071c\). Over a fixed distance the packet centre arrives about \(0.9003/0.7071=1.27\) times as late as a crest with that phase speed. A broadband pulse need not have one well-defined group speed.

Further reading · Fließbach, Kontinuumsmechanik · Tong, Phonons.

Chapter 17 · Proper time, momentum and a moving clock

A pair of light pulses lets observers compare clocks without assuming a universal time. Build the invariant interval and use it to calculate transit times and the energy exchanged by moving material.

Identify what every inertial observer can agree on

Assign coordinates \(x,t\) to events using rulers and synchronized clocks in an inertial laboratory. A light ray moving along the positive or negative axis obeys \(x=\pm ct\). A linear transformation between two inertial laboratories must take each family of light rays into itself if both measure the same \(c\). Introduce \(u=ct-x\) and \(w=ct+x\), coordinates constant on the two families. A boost rescales them. Reciprocity between inertial frames and spatial reflection give opposite rescalings,

\[u'=e^\eta u,\ w'=e^{-\eta}w.\]

Here the additive parameter \(\eta\) is called rapidity.

\[c^2t'^2-x'^2=u'w'=uw=c^2t^2-x^2.\]

Adding and subtracting the transformed coordinates gives

\[ct'=ct\cosh\eta-x\sinh\eta,\]
\[x'=x\cosh\eta-ct\sinh\eta.\]

The moving origin obeys \(x'=0\), so

\[v/c=\tanh\eta,\]
\[\cosh\eta=\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}.\]

These statements concern pairs of events. An experiment involving a rod must separately specify which endpoint events are simultaneous in the observer's frame.

Follow one clock along its trajectory

Events on the same material clock have \(dx'=0\) instantaneously in its rest frame. The invariant interval then gives

\[d\tau=dt\sqrt{1-v(t)^2/c^2}.\]

Over a curved path integrate this local relation. Two synchronized clocks reunited at the same event can have accumulated different proper times because their intervening paths differ.

Consider an inertially moving clock passing two fixed laboratory gates 12 light-microseconds apart. With \(v=0.80c\) the lab crossing interval is 15 µs. The travelling clock accumulates \(15/1.6667=9.0\) µs. It measures the simultaneous distance between gates in its own frame as 7.2 light-microseconds. Dividing that distance by \(0.80c\) gives the same 9.0 µs. Combining a laboratory distance with a clock time from another frame would obscure this check.

From a clock to energy and momentum

Differentiate the spacetime position with respect to the invariant proper time. The resulting four-velocity transforms as a four-vector. For a particle of constant rest mass \(m\), multiply by that mass to obtain the four-momentum \(p^\mu=(E/c,\mathbf p)=m\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\). The invariant norm is obtained in the rest frame and gives

\[E^2-p^2c^2=m^2c^4,\]
\[K=E-mc^2 .\]

For low speed, expanding \(\gamma\) returns \(K=mv^2/2\) to lowest order. For light, the massless relation \(E=pc\) holds without defining a rest frame. These elementary cases are useful checks when adding the four-momenta of a system.

Imagine two identical material samples with equal and opposite speeds \(0.60c\) close into a sealed calorimeter at rest in their centre-of-momentum frame. Ignoring the original container mass and any energy escaping, the total momentum vanishes and the invariant mass of the combined contents is \(2\gamma m=2.50m\). The excess \(0.50mc^2\) over the original rest energies is internal energy in this frame. Energy conservation applies throughout the process.

Vary the gate experiment

Increase speed at fixed laboratory gate separation. Predict both the coordinate time and the travelling clock's proper time. At a fixed speed, doubling the distance doubles both readings.

Open this experiment online

Tutorial on identifying the frame

A laboratory separates two gates by 24 light-microseconds. A travelling clock measures 18 µs between crossings. Determine the speed.

Work through the solution

In units with distance in light-microseconds, the lab time is \(24/\beta\) µs. The interval gives \(18^2=(24/\beta)^2-24^2\), so

\[\beta=24/30=0.800.\]

The laboratory time is 30 µs. This inversion uses one distance and two events without assuming the clocks display the same elapsed time.

An emission and reception have laboratory separation \(6\) light-microseconds and time difference \(10\,\mu\mathrm s\). Could one inertial clock record both, and which speed would it need?

Work through the solution

The interval is timelike because \(10^2-6^2=64>0\). The unique inertial path between the two events has speed \(0.6c\). Its measured time is \(8\,\mu\mathrm s\), consistent with \(10/\gamma\) and \(\gamma=1.25\). A laboratory separation of 12 light-microseconds at the same time difference would be spacelike and could not be joined by such a clock.

In the laboratory a single light pulse has energy \(E\) and momentum \(E/c\). Compare its invariant mass with that of two pulses of energy \(E\) travelling in opposite directions together as a system.

Work through the solution

For one pulse \(E^2-p^2c^2=0\). For the pair the energies add to \(2E\) and the vector momenta cancel. The system therefore has invariant mass \(2E/c^2\). The invariant mass of a composite system depends on total four-momentum. Individual invariant masses alone do not specify it.

Further reading · Fließbach, Relativistische Mechanik · Tong, Dynamics and Relativity, chapter 7.
