With \(p_*c=\beta E^*\), the laboratory longitudinal components are \(p_{1z}=\gamma p_*(1+\cos\theta_*)\) and \(p_{2z}=\gamma p_*(1-\cos\theta_*)\), and their transverse components are opposite with magnitude \(p_*\sin\theta_*\). The two lab polar angles therefore obey \(\tan\theta_1=\tan(\theta_*/2)/\gamma\) and \(\tan\theta_2=\cot(\theta_*/2)/\gamma\). Multiplying gives

\[\tan\theta_1\tan\theta_2=1/\gamma^2.\]

At low speed \(\gamma\to1\), so \(\theta_1+\theta_2\to90^\circ\). For finite boost the opening angle becomes smaller. Endpoint cases where one outgoing particle is stationary leave its direction undefined and must be handled separately.

Take rest energy \(\mathcal M\) and projectile kinetic energy \(K=2\mathcal M\) against an identical stationary target. The invariant energy is \(\sqrt8\mathcal M\) and the laboratory total energy is \(4\mathcal M\), giving \(\gamma_{\rm cm}=\sqrt2\). For a transverse centre-of-momentum collision, both products have laboratory angle \(\arctan(1/\sqrt2)=35.26^\circ\) on opposite sides of the beam, so the opening is \(70.53^\circ\). Both laboratory energies are \(2\mathcal M\); their kinetic energies are each \(\mathcal M\), sharing the incident kinetic energy equally. Angular data and energy partition together offer an overdetermined test of elastic equal-mass kinematics.

For a general \(\theta_*\), the lab kinetic-energy fractions are \([1+\cos\theta_*]/2\) and \([1-\cos\theta_*]/2\) of the incoming kinetic energy in this equal-mass geometry. This follows by inserting \(E^*=\gamma_{\rm cm}\mathcal M\) in the boost and using \(K=2\mathcal M(\gamma_{\rm cm}^2-1)\). Equal masses do not imply equal final energies in the laboratory; that occurs for the transverse centre-of-momentum geometry. A detector threshold of \(0.25K\) on both products selects \(|\cos\theta_*|\le0.50\). For an isotropic momentum-frame distribution that condition accepts half the events irrespective of the azimuth, provided the lab apparatus covers both directions.

Compare two methods of estimating missing invariant mass

Suppose a known laboratory total has energy \(5.0\,{\rm GeV}\) and axial momentum times \(c\) of \(3.0\,{\rm GeV}\). One registered product has energy \(2.0\,{\rm GeV}\), longitudinal momentum times \(c\) of \(1.0\,{\rm GeV}\), and transverse momentum times \(c\) of \(0.60\,{\rm GeV}\). Subtracting vectors gives missing energy \(3.0\,{\rm GeV}\), axial momentum times \(c\) of \(2.0\,{\rm GeV}\), and transverse momentum times \(c\) of \(-0.60\,{\rm GeV}\). Its invariant mass energy is

\[\sqrt{9-4-0.36}=2.154\,{\rm GeV}.\]

Dropping the transverse measurement would give \(2.236\,{\rm GeV}\), an error of about \(3.8\%\). Subtracting reported kinetic energies instead of total energies would introduce an uncontrolled rest-energy offset.

The same result can be reconstructed in the initial centre-of-momentum frame. The total invariant energy is \(4.0\,{\rm GeV}\), so the laboratory boost is

\[\beta=0.60,\gamma=1.25.\]

Transforming the observed product back gives \(E^*=1.25(2.0-0.60\times1.0)=1.75\,{\rm GeV}\) and \(cp_z^*=1.25(1.0-0.60\times2.0)=-0.25\,{\rm GeV}\), while its transverse component stays \(0.60\,{\rm GeV}\). Missing energy is \(2.25\,{\rm GeV}\), and missing squared momentum times \(c^2\) is \(0.25^2+0.60^2\). The invariant is again \(4.64\,{\rm GeV^2}\). Repeating the computation in two frames checks signs and coordinate components without adding independent experimental information.

To propagate uncertainty use the squared quantity before taking its square root. With \(c=1\) for numerical units, perturbations satisfy

\[\delta M_{\rm miss}^2=2E_{\rm miss}\delta E_{\rm miss}-2\mathbf p_{\rm miss}\cdot\delta\mathbf p_{\rm miss}.\]

If the energy and momentum of one detected particle come from the same calibrated tracking measurement they may be strongly correlated. Treating those uncertainties as independent can seriously misestimate the spread, especially near a missing-mass threshold where \(M^2\) is close to zero. Retain the full covariance and report a distribution in mass squared near that boundary. Mapping negative noisy values to zero before averaging biases the result upward and erases information about detector resolution.

Recover a recoil energy from photon scattering

Consider an incoming photon of energy \(E\) colliding with a free particle of rest energy \(\mathcal M\) initially at rest. The outgoing photon has energy \(E'\) and turns through angle \(\theta\) in the original laboratory. Four-momentum conservation gives the final target energy \(\mathcal M+E-E'\) and its squared momentum times \(c^2\) is \(E^2+E'^2-2EE'\cos\theta\). Imposing the final target mass-shell condition and cancelling equal squares yields

\[\mathcal M(E-E')=EE'(1-\cos\theta).\]

Therefore

\[E'=\frac{E}{1+(E/\mathcal M)(1-\cos\theta)} .\]

The scattered energy equals the incident energy for perfect forward scattering, whereas backscattering transfers most energy at fixed incident \(E\). Rearrangement gives

\[1/E'-1/E=(1-\cos\theta)/\mathcal M.\]

Multiplying by \(hc\) gives the usual wavelength shift with scale \(h/(mc)\). The argument uses only four-momentum conservation and the initial target mass to determine kinematics. It does not give the probability of any scattering angle, which requires an interaction model. Bound target motion or initially moving scatterers change the measured line shape even when the elementary free-particle kinematics is understood.

Take \(E=\mathcal M/2\). At \(\theta=90^\circ\) the outgoing photon energy is \(\mathcal M/3\); at \(\theta=\pi\) it is \(\mathcal M/4\). In the right-angle event the target kinetic energy is

\[E-E'=\mathcal M/6.\]

Its final momentum magnitude times \(c\) can be computed from its energy as \(\sqrt{(7\mathcal M/6)^2-\mathcal M^2}=\sqrt{13}\mathcal M/6\), or from the photon momentum triangle as \(\sqrt{(\mathcal M/2)^2+(\mathcal M/3)^2}\). These two values agree. A detector that measures only target kinetic energy can infer the photon angle if the initial photon energy was known and the free stationary target assumptions hold.

The maximum possible target kinetic energy is \(2E^2/(\mathcal M+2E)\). For \(E\ll\mathcal M\) this is approximately \(2E^2/\mathcal M\), much smaller than the incident energy. At \(E\gg\mathcal M\) the recoiling target can receive most of the photon energy. Scanning incident energy therefore changes both the absolute and fractional accessible recoil range. If an observed event falls beyond that kinematic edge, changing only the angular cross section cannot explain it; examine energy calibration, initial target motion, coincidence assignment or overlapping events.

Identify what two unknown detector scales can be calibrated together

A two-body decay at rest into two photons yields equal energies and an opening angle of \(180^\circ\). In any frame its invariant parent rest energy is

\[M c^2=\sqrt{2E_1E_2(1-\cos\alpha)}.\]

This formula remains valid when the parent moves and the detected photon energies differ. A common multiplicative energy calibration factor multiplies the reconstructed mass by that factor. An angular bias also changes the inferred mass, with fractional derivative \(\tfrac12\sin\alpha/(1-\cos\alpha)=\tfrac12\cot(\alpha/2)\). Nearly collinear photon pairs are therefore particularly sensitive to angular uncertainties, even when their individual energy measurements are accurate.

For \(E_1=2.0\,{\rm GeV}\), \(E_2=1.0\,{\rm GeV}\), \(\alpha=60^\circ\), the reconstructed rest energy is \(\sqrt2\,{\rm GeV}\), although the lab energy sum is \(3.0\,{\rm GeV}\). A one-degree positive error in the opening angle changes the inferred mass by approximately \(0.5\cot30^\circ(\pi/180)=1.51\%\). Measuring events with a range of opening angles can distinguish an angular offset from a common energy-scale factor, since the latter has no such angular amplification. A calibration performed only on back-to-back pairs is weakly sensitive to opening-angle errors to first order.

Invariant reconstruction is especially valuable when different observers disagree on which laboratory particle appears fast or forward. Agreement requires the entire event be expressed in one frame, with coincident incoming and outgoing measurements and a consistent sign convention for momentum. A Lorentz transformation cannot repair a mispaired event. Estimate statistical backgrounds and detector resolution independently before interpreting a narrow or displaced mass feature. The invariant provides a kinematic check; it gains physical meaning from the measurement model used to construct it.

Reconstruct a two-body decay with a nonzero boost

A parent with known rest energy \(W\) decays into one massive daughter of rest energy \(m_d c^2\) and one photon. In the parent rest frame the common momentum magnitude follows from the two-body formula, so photon energy is

\[E_\gamma^*=[W^2-(m_d c^2)^2]/(2W).\]

For a moving parent, the lab photon energy spans a range depending on the emission angle:

\[E_\gamma=\gamma E_\gamma^*(1+\beta\cos\theta_*).\]

The end energies \(E_{\max},E_{\min}\) for emission forward and backward have product \((E_\gamma^*)^2\) and ratio \((1+\beta)/(1-\beta)\). Thus a measured energy band can give both the rest-frame line energy and the parent speed if its full angular range is observed and all parents share a common boost.

Take \(W=3.0\,{\rm GeV}\),

\[m_dc^2=1.0\,{\rm GeV}.\]

The rest-frame photon energy is \(4/3\,{\rm GeV}\). With \(\beta=0.60,\gamma=1.25\), the accessible lab endpoints are \(2.667\) and \(0.667\,{\rm GeV}\). Their geometric mean recovers \(1.333\,{\rm GeV}\), and \((E_{\max}-E_{\min})/(E_{\max}+E_{\min})=0.600\) recovers the boost. The total energy released as rest energy difference is \(2.0\,{\rm GeV}\), larger than the photon energy in the rest frame because the massive daughter must recoil. Assigning all the rest-energy difference to radiation ignores that conserved momentum even before any laboratory transformation.

If the parent decays isotropically in its rest frame, \(\cos\theta_*\) is uniformly distributed. The linear photon-energy relation then gives a flat lab energy density between the endpoints when every direction is detected with equal efficiency and the parent boost is fixed. A laboratory detector covering only a forward cone selects part of the interval and can produce an apparently shifted line or a nonuniform spectrum. A spread of parent speeds superposes intervals with different endpoints. Before interpreting spectral width as an intrinsic lifetime or a spread in masses, separate angular acceptance, boost distribution and instrumental resolution.

The lab photon angle obeys \(\cos\theta_{\rm lab}=(\cos\theta_*+\beta)/(1+\beta\cos\theta_*)\). At transverse rest-frame emission \(\cos\theta_*=0\), the lab photon points at about \(53.1^\circ\) for the stated boost. Its energy is \(1.667\,{\rm GeV}\). The corresponding massive daughter has a different aberration relation because its rest-frame speed is below \(c\). A photon angle formula should not be reused for a massive track. Transform its actual four-vector to draw the two lab directions and compare them with the expected missing momentum of the unobserved partner.

Compare elapsed times along different trajectories

Study proper time and laboratory coordinate time for the same motion. Identify the invariant clock interval before comparing a measurement between frames.

Open this experiment online

Audit a relativistic event using dimensionless rapidity

For one-dimensional motion define rapidity \(y\) by \(E=mc^2\cosh y,\ cp=mc^2\sinh y\). Then \(v/c=\tanh y\) and collinear boosts add or subtract rapidities. The invariant for two collinear massive particles becomes

\[s=\mathcal M_1^2+\mathcal M_2^2+2\mathcal M_1\mathcal M_2\cosh(y_1-y_2).\]

The available energy depends on their relative rapidity, not on their common boost. At very high same-direction energies, constructing \(E_{\rm total}^2-(cp_{\rm total})^2\) can lose floating-point precision through subtraction. Expressing the input with known rest energies and relative rapidity can be numerically better conditioned.

For two equal masses at rapidities \(3.0\) and \(2.0\),

\[\sqrt s=2\mathcal M\cosh(0.5)=2.2553\mathcal M.\]

A common boost adding ten to both leaves this value unchanged even though each lab energy grows by orders of magnitude. Their centre-of-momentum rapidity is \(2.5\) in the initial frame because equal masses at rapidities \(\pm0.5\) have opposite momenta. A particle starting at rapidity three appears to move only at \(\tanh(0.5)=0.462c\) in that frame. This separates a very large laboratory kinetic energy from a modest relative collision energy.

A computation obtains slightly negative \(s\) for two very energetic nearly parallel massive tracks, even though both individual four-vectors were formed from positive masses. What calculation can distinguish rounding from a physical inconsistency?

Work through the solution

Recalculate using independently measured directions and rest masses. For a track of known momentum magnitude, evaluate \(E-cp=\mathcal M^2/(E+cp)\) so that a small positive difference is recovered without subtracting nearly equal large numbers. In a collinear test use the rapidity expression; at nonzero angle separate the positive angular term \(c^2p_1p_2(1-\cos\alpha)\), with \(1-\cos\alpha=2\sin^2(\alpha/2)\). Compare with higher precision and propagated measurement covariance. For ideal future-directed massive four-vectors their total cannot be spacelike, so a stable negative value would indicate inconsistent measured inputs or a reconstruction error rather than a new kinematic channel.

Choose a laboratory energy convention for published event tables

An event table may label one column beam energy while another experiment quotes beam kinetic energy for the same particle. The distinction is a full rest energy. For a stationary equal-mass target, inserting total projectile energy \(E_{\rm proj}\) gives

\[s=2\mathcal M^2+2\mathcal M E_{\rm proj};\]

inserting kinetic energy \(K\) requires

\[s=4\mathcal M^2+2\mathcal M K.\]

At a quoted numerical beam value \(2\mathcal M\) the two interpretations yield centre-of-momentum energies \(\sqrt6\,\mathcal M\) and \(\sqrt8\,\mathcal M\), distinct enough to change whether a final channel is kinematically open.

Before comparing two angular or energy spectra, record which particle was initially at rest, the energy convention, whether angles refer to the momentum frame or laboratory, and which particles passed the selection. Each changes an equation already derived above. A sample with a laboratory energy cut can acquire a forward asymmetry even if the underlying centre-of-momentum scattering is perfectly isotropic. Mapping every selected event back to the momentum frame without also correcting the angle-dependent acceptance will preserve that selection bias. The conserved invariant determines the accessible final kinematics; the detector determines which part of that set becomes visible.

Tutorial on collision measurements

At fixed-target energy \(K=0.020\mathcal M\), compare the available kinetic energy above the two incoming rest energies in the momentum frame with the Newtonian reduced-mass prediction.

Work through the solution

Expansion gives

\[\sqrt s=2\mathcal M\sqrt{1+K/(2\mathcal M)}\simeq2\mathcal M+K/2-K^2/(16\mathcal M).\]

The leading available energy is half the lab projectile kinetic energy, as for two equal Newtonian masses with one at rest. The correction here is \(0.000025\mathcal M\), about one quarter percent of the leading available kinetic energy. An energy expansion must subtract the rest-energy offset before calculating a relative error.

Two photons of equal energy \(E_\gamma\) intersect at angle \(\alpha\). Derive the total centre-of-momentum energy, including the parallel and antiparallel limits.

Work through the solution

The mass-shell terms vanish and the spatial momenta have magnitude \(E_\gamma/c\). Thus

\[s=2E_\gamma^2(1-\cos\alpha)=4E_\gamma^2\sin^2(\alpha/2).\]

Parallel rays have a null total and zero invariant energy, although laboratory energy is \(2E_\gamma\). Opposing rays have zero net momentum and centre-of-momentum energy \(2E_\gamma\). A relative closing rate is not the invariant energy.

An unknown neutral product escapes an otherwise recorded two-body event. Which four-vector combination should a detector reconstruct, and what does a negative inferred mass squared suggest?

Work through the solution

Subtract the measured final four-momenta from the known incoming total and square the missing four-vector with the stated metric. A single missing physical massive product gives its positive rest mass squared after the appropriate powers of \(c\); a massless one gives zero. A significantly negative result indicates an inconsistent reconstruction, an unaccounted incoming momentum, event mismatch or measurement bias. Multiple escaping products generally yield their combined invariant mass and cannot be identified uniquely from that scalar alone.

Analytical mechanics from constraints to invariants · 13. Which path is shortest across the surface of a cone?

A point can move along a conical surface while its azimuth and height both change. Unroll the geometry and predict the shortest path between two marked points. The measurable minimum radius distinguishes the geodesic from a line drawn along a horizontal circle.

Turn the constraint into a distance measurement

Let \(r\) denote the slant distance from the apex and \(\alpha\) the angle between the cone's side and its central axis. A point at \(r\) lies on a horizontal circle of radius \(r\sin\alpha\). Small radial and azimuthal displacements on the surface meet at right angles. Their squared distance adds to \(ds^2=dr^2+r^2\sin^2\alpha\,d\phi^2\). The change of variable \(\psi=\phi\sin\alpha\) turns this into the polar metric of a plane. Cutting the cone along a generator and flattening it produces a sector of opening angle \(2\pi\sin\alpha\).

Without a tangential force a particle follows a straight line in the unrolled sector. Its coordinates need not evolve linearly in the original azimuth. For two positions at equal slant distance \(R\) separated by physical azimuth \(\Delta\phi\) of magnitude at most \(\pi\), the shortest branch uses a straight chord spanning \(\Delta\psi=\sin\alpha\,\Delta\phi\). Bisecting the isosceles triangle gives

\[L=2R\sin(|\Delta\psi|/2),\]
\[r_{\min}=R\cos(\Delta\psi/2).\]

The other copies of the endpoint correspond to winding around the cone on different branches. The chord formula uses a branch reached without passing through the apex. When the physical endpoints are diametrically opposite, clockwise and anticlockwise branches have equal shortest length. A laboratory string stretched across the interior would use the three-dimensional chord, which need not stay on the surface.

Detect the departure from the horizontal ring

For a cone of half-angle 30 degrees, two marks 120 degrees apart at slant distance 5 cm appear only 60 degrees apart in the plane. Their shortest surface path is 5.00 cm long and passes through radius 4.33 cm. Staying on the horizontal ring would require \(R\Delta\psi=5.24\) cm. The straight three-dimensional chord between the same marks is only 4.33 cm long but cuts through the cone. Comparing those three lengths distinguishes a free-space displacement from two distinct constrained motions.

Exercise · infer the slope

Two marks at slant distance 10 cm and azimuth separation 120 degrees have a geodesic of length 10 cm. What is the cone half-angle?

Work through the solution

The measured chord gives

\[\sin(\Delta\psi/2)=10/(2\cdot10)=1/2.\]

The shortest branch has \(\Delta\psi=60^\circ\), hence \(\sin\alpha=60/120=1/2\) and \(\alpha=30^\circ\). Use the same angular units in the ratio.

Exercise · compare with a weakly curved path

Find the relative excess of ring length over geodesic for a small unrolled separation \(\delta\). Why does a very small patch look flat?

Work through the solution

Expanding \(2\sin(\delta/2)=\delta-\delta^3/24+\cdots\) gives

\[(R\delta-L)/(R\delta)=\delta^2/24+O(\delta^4).\]

Both paths have the same tangent at leading order. The cone away from its apex is intrinsically developable; the small difference here measures the curvature of the chosen ring inside that developed plane.

Analytical mechanics from constraints to invariants · 14. Motion in a medium and momentum carried across a boundary

Two beads can approach exactly the same terminal speed with recognisably different histories. A sand cart can slow down while the total horizontal momentum of sand and cart stays fixed. Both observations begin by specifying which material the equation of motion follows.

Infer the force law from a falling bead

Choose downward displacement as positive. A submerged bead of volume \(V\), density \(\rho_b\) and mass \(m\) displaces fluid of density \(\rho_f\). In a fluid initially at rest the static pressure gradient supplies buoyancy \(\rho_f Vg\). Combine the two constant forces into \(m g_e=(\rho_b-\rho_f)Vg\). Assume a heavy bead, negligible wall effects and sufficiently slow changes to neglect added mass and viscous memory. A drag law must reverse sign when the velocity changes sign.

\[m\dot v=mg_e-bv,\]
\[m\dot v=mg_e-c|v|v.\]

In the first model \(b\) has units kg/s, in the second \(c\) has units kg/m. Equating drag to the effective weight gives \(v_\infty=mg_e/b\) or \(v_\infty=\sqrt{mg_e/c}\). Near zero speed both models give initial acceleration \(g_e\). Equal initial slope and equal terminal speed therefore leave the force law undetermined.

Solve both initial-value problems

Choose the characteristic time \(\tau=v_\infty/g_e\) and write \(u=v/v_\infty\), \(s=t/\tau\). Starting from rest the positive-speed branches obey \(du/ds=1-u\) and \(du/ds=1-u^2\). Separation and integration from zero give \(-\ln(1-u)=s\) and \(\operatorname{artanh}u=s\). A second integration supplies displacements that a camera can measure directly.

\[u_{\rm lin}=1-e^{-s},\]
\[z_{\rm lin}=v_\infty\tau(s-1+e^{-s}).\]
\[u_{\rm quad}=\tanh s,\]
\[z_{\rm quad}=v_\infty\tau\ln(\cosh s).\]

To start a data analysis, fit the early displacement to \(g_e t^2/2\) and determine the late speed independently. After this scaling, each curve is a prediction with no free fitting amplitude. With \(g_e=9.81\) m/s² and \(v_\infty=3.0\) m/s the time scale is 0.306 s. The competing predictions already differ by about 0.39 m/s at 0.30 s.

Recall · Which drag law has a mechanical basis here?

For a rigid sphere of radius \(a\) moving slowly in a Newtonian fluid the creeping-flow result is \(b=6\pi\eta a\). Check \(\mathrm{Re}=2a\rho_f|v|/\eta\) throughout the run. When inertia matters a pressure-drag model uses \(c=\rho_f C_D A/2\) with frontal area \(A\). Treating \(C_D\) as constant requires a range in which it varies slowly.

This browser calculation implements RK4 directly. The notebook below runs the same initial-value problem with OneSimulation; set its terminal, g and step to the displayed values to reproduce the comparison. The constant-coefficient drag assumptions still apply.

Open this experiment online

Reproduce with OneSimulation

Change the terminal speed and the time step. Compare the entire computed trace with the exact quadratic result, then identify where the two force models separate most visibly.

Run the downloaded notebook with OneSimulation, NumPy and Matplotlib installed. The output below was recorded with the displayed calculation.

"""Drop a bead from rest in two media with equal terminal speeds."""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from onesim.numerics.time import ClassicalRungeKutta4TimeIntegrator

g, terminal = 9.81, 3.0  # effective downward acceleration and terminal speed
step = 0.01
time = np.arange(151) * step
method = ClassicalRungeKutta4TimeIntegrator()

def rates(speed, t):
    linear, quadratic = speed
    return (g * (1 - linear / terminal),
            g * (1 - quadratic * abs(quadratic) / terminal**2))

speeds = [(0.0, 0.0)]
for t in time[:-1]:
    speeds.append(method.advance(speeds[-1], rates, step, time=t))
linear, quadratic = np.array(speeds).T
exact = terminal * np.tanh(g * time / terminal)
print(f"At 0.30 s: linear {linear[30]:.4f} m/s, quadratic {quadratic[30]:.4f} m/s")
print(f"Largest RK4 discrepancy for quadratic drag: {max(abs(exact-quadratic)):.2e} m/s")
plt.plot(time, linear, label="Linear drag")
plt.plot(time, quadratic, label="Quadratic drag")
plt.axhline(terminal, linestyle=":", color="grey", label="Terminal speed")
plt.xlabel("Time after release (s)")
plt.ylabel("Downward speed (m/s)")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("physics-drag-laws.png", dpi=160)

Computed output

At 0.30 s: linear 1.8752 m/s, quadratic 2.2605 m/s
Largest RK4 discrepancy for quadratic drag: 5.18e-08 m/s

Derive the equation for a changing collection of matter

Let a horizontal cart of instantaneous mass \(M\) and speed \(v\) collect grains at rate \(\dot M>0\). Just before collection a small parcel \(dM\) has horizontal laboratory velocity \(w\). Over \(dt\) the momentum of cart plus parcel changes by the external impulse. The incoming parcel is included on the initial side so that the comparison follows the same matter.

\[Mv+w\,dM+F_{\rm ext}\,dt=(M+dM)(v+dv).\]

Drop the product \(dM\,dv\), divide by time and keep the finite acceleration. The relative speed determines how strongly the intake changes the cart velocity.

\[M\dot v=F_{\rm ext}+(w-v)\dot M,\]
\[\frac{d(Mv)}{dt}=F_{\rm ext}+w\dot M.\]

Take a 20 kg cart rolling at 3 m/s on a level frictionless track. Grains falling vertically carry zero horizontal momentum. After collecting 10 kg, the common speed is 2 m/s. The horizontal kinetic energy falls from 90 J to 60 J. The collisions can dissipate energy even though the horizontal external impulse vanishes. The vertical momentum and gravitational energy belong to a separate balance.

Recall · Moving boundaries and signs

The formula uses laboratory-frame \(w\) immediately outside the cart and signed mass rate into the cart. For outflow use the velocity of matter as it leaves. A leaking cart with material departing at the cart's horizontal speed has no resulting horizontal acceleration.

Tutorial on identifying a mechanical system

1 · When do the two beads reach 90% of the terminal speed?

Work through the solution

The dimensionless times are \(\ln 10=2.303\) and \(\operatorname{artanh}(0.9)=1.472\). At the stated parameters these are 0.704 s and 0.450 s. An early-velocity measurement distinguishes the laws more efficiently than another terminal-speed estimate.

2 · Infer an intake speed from a measured acceleration

Work through the solution

A 12 kg cart moving at 1.5 m/s gains 0.40 kg/s and accelerates at 0.020 m/s² along a level frictionless track. From \(w=v+M\dot v/\dot M\) the grains enter at 2.10 m/s. Using \(F=d(Mv)/dt\) without an inlet flux would falsely infer an external force.

3 · Test a radius scaling before fitting a drag coefficient

Work through the solution

For spheres of the same density, effective weight scales as \(a^3\). Stokes drag then predicts \(v_\infty\propto a^2\). At fixed \(C_D\), quadratic drag gives \(v_\infty\propto a^{1/2}\). Doubling radius gives speed ratios 4 and \(\sqrt2\). Check Reynolds numbers, wall clearances and bead density before inferring a force law.

For further study see Taylor, Classical Mechanics, chapters 1–4 on force laws, dissipative motion and momentum transport.

Analytical mechanics from constraints to invariants · 15. From a repeating trajectory to a chaotic attractor

A damped pendulum under a periodic drive can settle into the same orbit on each run yet visit a different point on successive drive periods. A return map supplies the right clock for distinguishing a new period from a slowly decaying transient.

Build a map from a continuous mechanical experiment

Consider a pendulum with dimensionless time in units of its small-angle period divided by \(2\pi\). Let \(q\) be the positive damping rate, \(A\) the drive amplitude and \(\omega\) the drive frequency.

\[\dot\theta=p,\]
\[\dot p=-q p-\sin\theta+A\cos(\omega t).\]

Prepare all observations at drive phase zero and evolve for \(T=2\pi/\omega\). The stroboscopic map takes \((\theta_n,p_n)\) to \((\theta_{n+1},p_{n+1})\). Complete rotations can be plotted modulo \(2\pi\) while the unwrapped angle tracks transport. An attracting period-one orbit appears as one point after transients. A period-two orbit alternates between two points and returns after \(2T\).

For a small patch in the state plane the instantaneous fractional area growth is the divergence \(\partial_\theta p+\partial_p\dot p=-q\). Integration over a period gives a Jacobian determinant \(e^{-qT}\). Phase-area contraction allows an attractor. A periodically driven Hamiltonian system at \(q=0\) instead has a unit determinant.

Recall · Why use a section at fixed drive phase?

Two trajectories with identical angle and speed can accelerate differently at different phases of an external drive. Sampling once per drive period compares equal external conditions. Recording at a nearby period can turn a perfectly regular response into an apparent cloud of points.

Calculate a period doubling in a solvable map

Near a flip bifurcation with only one slow direction, a one-dimensional map helps explain stability changes. The logistic map \(f(x)=rx(1-x)\) on \(0\leq x\leq1\) for \(0<r\leq4\) is an illustrative return law. Its \(r\) is not a calibrated pendulum torque. An interior fixed point is \(x_*=1-1/r\). For a small displacement \(\delta_{n+1}\simeq f'(x_*)\delta_n\), giving a multiplier \(2-r\). Its magnitude crosses one at \(r=3\) with negative sign.

To find the new orbit, solve \(f(f(x))-x=0\) and remove the two fixed-point factors \(x\) and \(x-x_*\). The remaining quadratic has roots

\[x_\pm=\frac{r+1\pm\sqrt{(r-3)(r+1)}}{2r}.\]

Its two-step multiplier is \(f'(x_+)f'(x_-)=-r^2+2r+4\). At \(r=3.2\) it is 0.16 and deviations fall by that factor every two observations. At \(r=1+\sqrt6\) it reaches \(-1\), so that orbit loses stability. Additional doublings create intervals of higher-period motion. Periodic windows interrupt the chaotic parameter range.

Try it · Logistic

Change the inputs and compare the recalculated curves with the preceding derivation and baseline figure. The axes give the units; the numerical readout states the model assumptions and any limiting cases. Reset the inputs to return to the reference setting.

Open this live calculation

Estimate a growth rate while keeping the observations bounded

A separation eventually saturates at the attractor size. To estimate growth over many periods, multiply the local tangent factors and take a logarithm before averaging. Along a sampled orbit the largest exponent of the scalar map is

\[\lambda_N=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\ln\left|r(1-2x_j)\right|.\]

For \(r=4\) the substitution \(x=\sin^2\phi\) maps an iteration to angle doubling modulo the symmetries of the sine. Typical invariant-measure trajectories have \(\lambda=\ln2\) per iteration. Exceptional exact initial conditions, including a critical point that maps onto zero, do not estimate that typical value. Finite precision eventually creates repetitions. Report the sampling window and discard transient returns.

For a mechanical test, integrate two nearby pendulum trajectories, sample at \(T\), rescale the difference back to its small original norm and accumulate its log growth. Repeat with smaller time step and different starting points in the same basin. A positive long-time exponent and recurrent bounded motion are distinct pieces of evidence. Slow beats and noisy sensors can broaden a spectrum without deterministic chaos.

Tutorial on return maps

1 · Predict the number of observed return points

Work through the solution

For \(r=3.2\), the roots of the two-cycle are about 0.5130 and 0.7995. Check directly that the first maps near 0.7995. Two sensor samples cannot distinguish a two-cycle from a transient. Repeated pairs should approach these values with the calculated two-step multiplier.

2 · Separate dissipation from instability

Work through the solution

For \(qT=0.4\) the area factor is 0.6703. If one real multiplier of a period-one orbit is \(-1.2\), its partner is \(0.6703/(-1.2)=-0.559\). The orbit expands along one direction despite contracting area in total.

3 · Design a finite-time comparison

Work through the solution

An apparent doubling every three drive periods corresponds to \(\ln2/3=0.231\) per return. Repeat the estimate with several initial separations above roundoff and below the nonlinear scale, increase the observation window and verify persistence when the numerical step is halved.

For further study see Taylor, Classical Mechanics, chapters 11–12 on nonlinear oscillations, the driven pendulum and chaos.

Analytical mechanics from constraints to invariants · 16. From differential acceleration to three-dimensional strain and stress

An accelerometer in a falling laboratory can read zero while a pair of falling test masses moves apart. A crystal can support different longitudinal and transverse speeds in the same direction. Both measurements require the spatial variation of a vector field, represented by a tensor.

Derive the relative acceleration in a falling frame

Let a laboratory origin fall freely at position \(\mathbf R\) in the field \(\mathbf g(\mathbf R)=-GM\mathbf R/R^3\) of a spherical source. Over a small separation \(\boldsymbol\xi\) choose parallel nonrotating axes. Subtract the origin's acceleration and expand to first order:

\[\ddot\xi_i=g_i(\mathbf R+\boldsymbol\xi)-g_i(\mathbf R)\simeq T_{ij}\xi_j,\]
\[T_{ij}=\frac{GM}{R^3}(3n_i n_j-\delta_{ij}),\]
\[\mathbf n=\mathbf R/R.\]

The radial eigenvalue is \(2GM/R^3\). Both transverse eigenvalues are \(-GM/R^3\). Outside the source the sum vanishes as required by \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf g=0\). Over a short time the fractional change of an initially stationary separation along an eigenvector is \(T_i t^2/2\). Near Earth's surface \(g/R\simeq1.54\times10^{-6}\) s⁻². Free masses initially separated by 2 m radially acquire a relative acceleration near \(6.2\) µm/s².

Recall · Which frame cancels gravity?

The origin's uniform acceleration cancels at all test masses when forming the difference. A rotating frame contributes centrifugal and Coriolis terms as well. For a small free-fall experiment state how axes are maintained and which relative velocities were initially present.

Try it · Tidal

Change the inputs and compare the recalculated curves with the preceding derivation and baseline figure. The axes give the units; the numerical readout states the model assumptions and any limiting cases. Reset the inputs to return to the reference setting.

Open this live calculation

Compare nearby material points before and after a displacement

Label a reference point by \(\mathbf X\) and let its displacement be \(\mathbf u(\mathbf X)\). An initial segment \(d\mathbf X\) becomes \((I+\nabla\mathbf u)d\mathbf X\). Expand its squared length, retaining the first-order terms. The antisymmetric part drops out of the quadratic form for length change.

\[d\ell'^2-d\ell^2=2\,dX_i\,\varepsilon_{ij}\,dX_j,\]
\[\varepsilon_{ij}=\tfrac12(\partial_i u_j+\partial_j u_i).\]

The trace gives fractional volume change. A rigid translation has zero displacement gradient. An infinitesimal rotation has an antisymmetric gradient, so it has zero linear strain as well. For simple shear \(u_x=\gamma y\) the component \(\varepsilon_{xy}=\gamma/2\) explains the factor of two between tensor and engineering shear strain.

Build Hooke's law from symmetries and an energy

On a cut normal to \(\mathbf n\), force per area is the traction \(t_i=\sigma_{ij}n_j\). Balancing moments in a continuum without intrinsic body couples gives symmetric Cauchy stress. In an initially unstressed isotropic linear solid a quadratic elastic energy can depend only on the two independent rotationally invariant quadratic forms of the strain.

\[W=\tfrac12\lambda(\operatorname{tr}\varepsilon)^2+\mu\,\varepsilon_{ij}\varepsilon_{ij},\]
\[\sigma_{ij}=\partial W/\partial\varepsilon_{ij}=\lambda\operatorname{tr}\varepsilon\,\delta_{ij}+2\mu\varepsilon_{ij}.\]

Under uniform dilation \(\varepsilon=\eta I\) the bulk modulus is \(K=\lambda+2\mu/3\). Pure shear isolates \(\mu\). Stability requires \(K>0\) and \(\mu>0\). The general anisotropic relation \(\sigma_{ij}=C_{ijkl}\varepsilon_{kl}\) need not reduce to two constants. Crystal symmetry decides which entries can be determined by rotating a sound measurement.

Recover both moduli from two arrival times

Balance of linear momentum gives \(\rho\ddot u_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}\) in a homogeneous body with no body force. A plane longitudinal displacement has nonzero divergence. A transverse displacement has zero divergence. Substitution gives their phase speeds:

\[c_L^2=(K+4\mu/3)/\rho,\]
\[c_T^2=\mu/\rho.\]

For a solid of density 2500 kg/m³ with \(c_L=5000\) m/s and \(c_T=3000\) m/s the two moduli are \(\mu=22.5\) GPa and \(K=32.5\) GPa. One longitudinal speed would determine only their combination. Short wavelengths comparable with the lattice spacing, or waves in a thin guide, require dispersion or geometric corrections before using these bulk equations.

Tutorial on differential measurements

1 · Recover a missing tidal eigenvalue

Work through the solution

Two transverse values measured outside a spherical source are each \(-1.5\times10^{-6}\) s⁻². Zero trace implies a radial value \(+3.0\times10^{-6}\) s⁻². A positive radial gradient means the higher test mass falls slightly less quickly.

2 · A diagonal cut through a sheared specimen

Work through the solution

Let only \(\sigma_{xy}=\sigma_{yx}=4\) MPa be nonzero. With \(\mathbf n=(1,1,0)/\sqrt2\), traction is \(4\mathbf n\) MPa. The same stress state that is pure shear on coordinate planes becomes a purely normal traction on this cut.

3 · Test isotropic elasticity using an additional wave

Work through the solution

If \(c_T\) differs systematically for two orthogonal transverse polarisations at the same direction and frequency, a homogeneous isotropic bulk model predicts the wrong degeneracy. Check the sample dimensions and alignment first, then measure crystal orientation before assigning a distinct shear modulus.

For further study see Taylor, Classical Mechanics, chapters 9 and 16 on noninertial observers and elastic continua.

Mechanics in the laboratory

Turn a measured trajectory or force into a test of a mechanical law. Derive the observable, propagate it numerically and determine which parameters the experiment can resolve.

  1. Measure gravity with a pendulum of finite amplitude

    A metre-long pendulum is an appealing clock because its small-angle period depends only on length and gravity. A precise clock can nevertheless give a precisely wrong value of gravity. Derive the full period, trace the systematic error to an identifiable approximation and design a measurement that distinguishes a length error from a release-angle error.

  2. Measure inertia and gravity with two suspension axes

    A rigid pendulum can oscillate from either of two knife edges. If the periods agree at distinct distances from the centre of mass, the spacing of the edges determines gravity. Derive the cancellation, identify a second way equal periods can arise and find why a poorly chosen geometry magnifies timing errors.

  3. Distinguish a physical precession from numerical drift

    A bound orbit circulates many times about its centre. A small change in the angle of successive closest approaches could be physical or could be accumulated phase error. Construct an exactly solvable family of precessing orbits that lets the two effects be compared without assuming a reference trajectory from another code.

  4. Which track reaches a lower point first?

    A bead is released from rest and slides without friction along a track between two points. A straight track is shortest, yet another path can deliver the bead sooner. Derive the travel-time functional, solve its boundary problem and compare actual times while changing the horizontal distance independently of the vertical drop.

  5. When can shaking a support stabilise an upside-down pendulum?

    A rapidly oscillating pivot can stabilise a pendulum near its normally unstable upright orientation. Develop the slowly varying effective potential, test its assumptions with the full time-dependent equation and compare the observable that each calculation predicts.

  6. When does a smooth circular guide lose contact?

    A bead moves inside a vertical circular guide after receiving a known speed at the bottom. Predict whether it turns around, separates from the guide or completes the circle. A normal-force measurement can distinguish these outcomes before a simple top-height energy test can.

Mechanics in the laboratory · 1. Measure gravity with a pendulum of finite amplitude

A metre-long pendulum is an appealing clock because its small-angle period depends only on length and gravity. A precise clock can nevertheless give a precisely wrong value of gravity. Derive the full period, trace the systematic error to an identifiable approximation and design a measurement that distinguishes a length error from a release-angle error.

Define the measured length and time

Use a point bob on a massless, inextensible string attached to a fixed pivot. Let \(L\) be the distance from pivot to the bob's centre of mass, and \(\theta\) the signed departure from the downward vertical. For a rigid extended bob, rotational inertia about its own centre adds to \(mL^2\); a length measured to the bottom of the bob is neither of these dynamical lengths. Measure the elapsed time between successive crossings of a photogate in the same direction. Crossings in opposite directions give half of the period in a symmetric oscillation. A stationary turning point is a poor timing marker because the position error there produces a large time error.

At rest at the release angle \(\theta_0\), the energy is \(mgL(1-\cos\theta_0)\). At a later angle the speed is \(L|\dot\theta|\). Equating kinetic plus potential energy to the release value gives

\[\dot\theta^2=(2g/L)(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0).\]

Only a quarter cycle is needed. Inverting the angular speed and integrating from zero to \(\theta_0\) produces a square-root singularity at release. The period is finite since integrating the inverse square root over a small interval gives a square root.

Resolve the turning point before approximating

Write \(k=\sin(\theta_0/2)\) and substitute \(\sin(\theta/2)=k\sin u\). The vanishing square root cancels a factor \(\cos u\) from the differential. One obtains the complete elliptic integral of the first kind with modulus \(k\).

\[T=4\sqrt{\frac Lg}\,K(k),\]
\[K(k)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{du}{\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2u}}.\]

Expanding its integrand yields

\[K(k)=(\pi/2)(1+k^2/4+9k^4/64+\cdots).\]

Since \(k\simeq\theta_0/2\) at small amplitude, the first fractional period correction is \(\theta_0^2/16\) with angle in radians. It is positive. At larger amplitude the tangential component of gravity rises more slowly with angle than the linear restoring law predicts. The pendulum spends longer near the turns. Passing degrees directly into the quadratic correction would give nonsense even if the timer and recorded angle were perfect.

Infer the bias in gravity

Suppose the true acceleration is \(9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), the length is 1.000 m and the release angle is 30 degrees. The small-angle period is about 2.0061 s and the finite-amplitude period about 2.0410 s. Interpreting the longer measured period by the linear formula would give about \(9.48\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The fractional gravity error is about twice the fractional period error with opposite sign because gravity is inferred from \(T^{-2}\). Timing a hundred periods reduces random timing error but leaves this systematic shift.

The numerical curve evaluates the complete elliptic integral. It uses the arithmetic–geometric mean identity \(K(k)=\pi/[2\,\mathrm{AGM}(1,\sqrt{1-k^2})]\), so no sampled point sits on the turning point. The single-correction curve truncates the amplitude series after its first nonconstant term. Vary angle and length, comparing both the predicted period and the result a linear analysis would infer. Which change rescales both period curves together? Which changes their relative discrepancy?

Open this experiment online

Design a two-release check

For the same pendulum the ratio \(T(\theta_a)/T(\theta_b)=K(k_a)/K(k_b)\) cancels the unknown length and local gravity. Measure at two amplitudes before deciding whether to recalibrate the length. If the ratio agrees but both absolute times differ from prediction, check the effective length, clock rate and model of the bob. If the ratio changes during a decaying swing, record initial and final amplitudes for the timed sequence. The period associated with a long sequence is an average over its slowly changing amplitude. Substituting the initial angle throughout would overcorrect the measurement.

Tutorial

At small amplitude, what release angle gives a fractional period bias of approximately one part in a thousand?

Work through the solution

Set \(\theta_0^2/16=0.001\). This gives \(0.1265\) rad, about 7.25 degrees. The gravity bias from an uncorrected measurement would be approximately two parts in a thousand. A tolerance on one quantity is not automatically the same tolerance on the other.

A photogate records successive interruptions every 1.02 seconds for the metre pendulum. A calculation gives nearly four times local gravity. Identify one possible error in the observable.

Work through the solution

The gate may have counted both directions and returned a half period. Doubling that interval gives about 2.04 s. Because the inferred acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the period, the missing factor of two gives a factor of four.

Why does reducing the grid spacing in an integration of the linear equation fail to recover the finite-amplitude curve?

Work through the solution

Integration error vanishes as the step is refined, but the restoring torque in that equation is \(mgL\theta\). The true torque is \(mgL\sin\theta\). A converged numerical solution can therefore provide independent evidence of an inadequate physical approximation.

For the equation of motion, phase portrait and dissipation, see the MIT treatment of the simple pendulum.

Mechanics in the laboratory · 2. Measure inertia and gravity with two suspension axes

A rigid pendulum can oscillate from either of two knife edges. If the periods agree at distinct distances from the centre of mass, the spacing of the edges determines gravity. Derive the cancellation, identify a second way equal periods can arise and find why a poorly chosen geometry magnifies timing errors.

Torque about an offset pivot

Take a rigid body of mass \(m\) with parallel suspension axes perpendicular to its plane of oscillation. Its moment of inertia about the centre of mass is \(I_C=m\rho^2\); \(\rho\) is the radius of gyration. For a pivot a distance \(a>0\) from the centre, the parallel-axis theorem gives

\[I_a=m(\rho^2+a^2).\]

Gravity exerts torque \(-mga\sin\theta\). In the small-angle limit,

\[T_a^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{g}\frac{\rho^2+a^2}{a},\]
\[L_a=a+\frac{\rho^2}{a}.\]

Here \(L_a\) is the length of a point pendulum with the same period. It can lie beyond the physical centre of mass. A tap applied at this distance from a pivot gives the centre of percussion when the ideal instantaneous pivot reaction is to vanish. The same combination of mass distribution and geometry appears in an impulsive and in an oscillatory measurement because both depend on angular momentum about that pivot.

Match the periods and keep both algebraic branches

Put the second knife edge on the opposite side of the centre at distance \(b\). Equal periods require

\[a+\rho^2/a=b+\rho^2/b.\]

Rearrange before dividing by \(a-b\):

\[(a-b)\left(1-\frac{\rho^2}{ab}\right)=0.\]

Two equal distances always give equal periods. That branch provides no information about \(\rho\). If the distances are distinct, equality implies

\[\rho^2=ab.\]

Both equivalent lengths then equal \(a+b\), the directly measurable edge separation. For \(a=0.200\,\mathrm m,\ b=0.450\,\mathrm m,\ \rho=0.300\,\mathrm m\), the equivalent length is 0.650 m and both periods at standard laboratory gravity are about 1.62 s. A small value of \(a-b\) is an experimental warning sign, even if the observed equality is exceptionally clean.

Background · Can unequal release amplitudes imitate a mismatch between pivots?

A rigid pendulum about either knife edge obeys the same sine nonlinearity as a simple pendulum. To leading order in its release angle \(\theta\) in radians, the measured period exceeds the small-amplitude period by the fraction \(\theta^2/16\). At matched small-amplitude periods, measurements with amplitudes \(\theta_a,\theta_b\) therefore give

\[\frac{T_a-T_b}{T_0}\simeq\frac{\theta_a^2-\theta_b^2}{16}.\]

Releasing at 6° about the first edge and 2° about the other creates a fractional mismatch of about \(6.1\times10^{-4}\). For a two-second period this is 1.2 ms. Record the two amplitudes along with the timing data and reduce both periods to the same limit before moving the trim mass. Otherwise the trim can compensate a preparation error.

Extract gravity when the two measured periods differ

Multiply the first period equation by \(a\) and the second by \(b\). Subtract to eliminate \(\rho^2\). The exact small-angle result for unequal distances is

\[g=4\pi^2\,\frac{a^2-b^2}{aT_a^2-bT_b^2}.\]

At matched periods this reduces to the simple expression in terms of the edge spacing. The general formula involves a difference in its denominator. If \(a\) and \(b\) nearly coincide, the denominator is small and two independent timing errors subtract with poor relative precision. This is a property of the inverse measurement, even if computing each individual period is perfectly well conditioned.

Once \(g\) is known, use \(\rho^2=gaT_a^2/(4\pi^2)-a^2\) to recover the body inertia per unit mass. A negative value may indicate a wrong distance measured to the centre or a timing observable that is actually a half period. Verify the result using the second pivot and recover a separately predicted period after shifting a suspension point. A single successful cancellation is weaker than reproducing an additional measurement.

Move one knife edge in the experiment

Hold \(a=0.200\,\mathrm m\) fixed and vary both the radius of gyration and the second distance. The graph plots the period against the possible second distance. Before inspecting intersections, predict where the second match should lie as \(\rho\) grows. The dependence on distance has a minimum at \(b=\rho\) because effective length comprises a growing and a decreasing term.

Open this experiment online

With a finite oscillation amplitude, the physical pendulum has the same elliptic correction as a point pendulum of length \(L_a\), provided the body is rigid and the frictionless pivot stays fixed. Matching different amplitudes can bias the cancellation. Measuring both at the same small angle removes the leading difference, and extrapolating both to zero amplitude provides a check. Rotational compliance of the knife edge and a shifting centre of mass require a different model.

Tutorial

For \(a=0.240\) m and \(\rho=0.300\) m, where should the second distinct match occur and what length should be used in \(g=4\pi^2L/T^2\)?

Work through the solution

The second branch gives

\[b=0.0900/0.240=0.375\,\mathrm{m}.\]

Because the pivots straddle the centre of mass the equivalent length is 0.615 m.

Both pivots lie on the same side of the centre, at the same distances \(a,b\) as in the previous question. What changes in the cancellation?

Work through the solution

The periods depend on the magnitudes of the offsets, so equal periods still imply \(\rho^2=ab\) on the distinct branch. The sum \(a+b\) still gives the equivalent length, but the physical ruler distance between pivots is \(|a-b|\). The direct measurement shortcut relies on the chosen geometry.

Why does setting both axes exactly at the same distance make even noise-free measurements insufficient to determine both \(g\) and \(\rho\)?

Work through the solution

The two equations are then identical. For every positive choice of inertia radius the first period determines a corresponding value of gravity. Improving timing precision cannot provide the missing independent equation.

Connect the offset-pivot calculation to the rigid-body inertia chapter.

Mechanics in the laboratory · 3. Distinguish a physical precession from numerical drift

A bound orbit circulates many times about its centre. A small change in the angle of successive closest approaches could be physical or could be accumulated phase error. Construct an exactly solvable family of precessing orbits that lets the two effects be compared without assuming a reference trajectory from another code.

Replace time by the measured polar angle

A particle of mass \(m\) moves in a static central potential \(V(r)=-k/r+\alpha/(2r^2)\) with \(k>0\). The radial force is \(-k/r^2+\alpha/r^3\). Angular momentum \(L=mr^2\dot\phi\) is constant. Put \(u=1/r\) and differentiate with respect to \(\phi\), denoting this derivative by a prime. The identities \(\dot r=-(L/m)u'\) and \(\ddot r=-(L^2/m^2)u^2u''\) follow by the chain rule. Subtracting the centripetal term \(r\dot\phi^2=(L^2/m^2)u^3\) from radial acceleration gives Binet's equation.

\[u''+(1+\delta)u=\frac{mk}{L^2},\]
\[\delta=\frac{m\alpha}{L^2}.\]

The sign of the perturbation matters. Positive \(\alpha\) gives a repulsive short-range correction, increasing radial frequency per unit angle. A mildly negative correction decreases it. This family is a test potential; a measured nonzero advance in nature need not have this particular cause.

Read apses from a harmonic equation

For \(1+\delta>0\), write \(\nu=\sqrt{1+\delta}\), \(u_c=mk/[L^2(1+\delta)]\) and impose \(u(0)=u_c(1+e)\), \(u'(0)=0\) with \(0<e<1\). Then \(u=u_c[1+e\cos(\nu\phi)]\). The radial minimum corresponds to a maximum of \(u\). Its next occurrence is at angle \(2\pi/\nu\), so the change of line of apsides per radial period is

\[\Delta\omega=2\pi\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\delta}}-1\right).\]

For \(\delta=0.04\), successive pericentres rotate backwards by approximately 7.0 degrees. At \(\delta=0\) the Kepler ellipse closes. For a strictly circular orbit the algebraic radial frequency has a well-defined small-oscillation limit, but the direction of pericentre of the observed circle has no unique value. A nearly circular orbit therefore has a genuine experimental difficulty even when the integration is accurate.

Compute the bias of a discrete orbit exactly

Shift \(v=u-u_c\). On a uniform angular grid of spacing \(h\), the centred second difference gives

\[v_{j+1}=2v_j-v_{j-1}-(h\nu)^2v_j.\]

Insert the trial \(v_j=e^{ij\psi}\) and simplify:

\[\cos\psi=1-\tfrac12(h\nu)^2,\]
\[\nu_h=\frac{2}{h}\arcsin(h\nu/2).\]

The numerical mode oscillates if \(h\nu<2\). Inside that range it is too fast, since the arcsine exceeds its argument. A bounded orbit can thus accumulate a negative apsidal error. For an unperturbed Kepler case and a 30-degree grid, the numerical angular frequency is roughly 1.012. Treating this as a physical result would infer a retrograde precession of roughly four degrees per revolution. Refining \(h\) halves the angular step and quarters the leading error, because \(\nu_h=\nu+\nu^3h^2/24+\cdots\).

The experiment plots radial phase after multiple nominal revolutions and reports the implied apsidal angles. Vary the perturbation at fixed step first, then halve the step at fixed perturbation. Distinguish the discrepancy that persists in the continuum from the discrepancy that can be extrapolated away. Starting all curves at pericentre makes the phase convention identical.

Hold the force exactly Newtonian. Compare the accumulated numerical phase on a 30° grid and 6° grid. The exact radial phase stays at zero in both runs. Use the exported values to estimate how the phase error scales when the angular step is divided by five.

Open this experiment online

Tutorial

A measured radial period is 364 degrees of azimuthal advance. In this family, which sign of \(\alpha\) is indicated and what is \(\delta\)?

Work through the solution

The radial cycle takes more than 360 degrees, so the radial frequency per unit angle is below one. The inferred correction is attractive,

\[\delta=(360/364)^2-1\simeq-0.02186.\]

A simulation reports advances of −1.20, −0.60 and −0.45 degrees at successive halvings of the angular step. What leading continuum estimate follows?

Work through the solution

With second-order phase bias, the final difference 0.15 equals three times the remaining magnitude of that bias. Adding 0.05 to −0.45 gives −0.40 degrees. The earlier pair gives the same estimate. An additional refinement tests the assumed scaling.

Can a long observation of a closed numerically integrated orbit rule out a time-step error in the orbital period?

Work through the solution

No. Closure depends on a ratio of radial to azimuthal phase advances. Both may be biased in the same proportion. Independently time successive crossings and compare with an analytic period or a finer integration. Different observables can hide different errors.

The midpoint experiment shows the converse sign of phase error for another bounded integrator.

Mechanics in the laboratory · 4. Which track reaches a lower point first?

A bead is released from rest and slides without friction along a track between two points. A straight track is shortest, yet another path can deliver the bead sooner. Derive the travel-time functional, solve its boundary problem and compare actual times while changing the horizontal distance independently of the vertical drop.

Choose the coordinate appearing in the speed law

Let \(y\) increase downwards from the release point, \(x\) increase along the horizontal and \(g\) be uniform. A small frictionless bead conserves mechanical energy, so its speed at depth \(y\) is \(\sqrt{2gy}\). For a track expressed as \(y(x)\) the time element is line element divided by speed. Hence

\[T[y]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2g}}\int_0^X \sqrt{\frac{1+y'^2}{y}}\,dx,\]
\[y(0)=0,\]
\[y(X)=Y.\]

A straight line has distance \(\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}\) and component of acceleration \(gY/\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}\), giving \(T_{\mathrm{line}}=\sqrt{2(X^2+Y^2)/(gY)}\). The advantage of a steeper early path is to build speed at the part of the trajectory where the bead would otherwise remain slow. A path with a longer distance can take less time because distances at different depths cost different amounts of time.

Use a first integral to remove a differential equation

Write the integrand excluding its constant multiplier as \(F=\sqrt{1+y'^2}/\sqrt y\). Since it contains no explicit \(x\), the Euler–Lagrange equation implies \(F-y'F_{y'}=\) constant. Differentiating this expression with respect to \(x\) shows the cancellation explicitly:

\[dF/dx=F_y y'+F_{y'}y'';\]

the derivative of the second term removes \(F_{y'}y''\) and leaves \(y'(F_y-dF_{y'}/dx)=0\). Substituting the integrand gives \(y(1+y'^2)=2a\) for some positive length \(a\).

Set \(y=a(1-\cos u)\). On the descending part \(y'=\cot(u/2)\). Integrating \(dx=\tan(u/2)dy\) yields

\[x=a(u-\sin u).\]

The signed derivative continues through zero at \(u=\pi\) and produces an ascending segment for \(\pi<u<2\pi\). A track may pass below the final point, then climb towards it while spending speed acquired earlier.

Solve for the actual endpoint and clock reading

Divide the endpoint coordinates to eliminate \(a\). The angle \(u_f\) solves \((u_f-\sin u_f)/(1-\cos u_f)=X/Y\) on the first arch. The ratio starts at zero and increases without bound; bisection gives a robust root for positive finite \(X/Y\). Recover \(a=Y/(1-\cos u_f)\). Along the cycloid \(ds=2a\sin(u/2)du\), while \(v=2\sqrt{ga}\sin(u/2)\). Their ratio is finite even at the cusp where both vanish:

\[T_{\mathrm{cyc}}=u_f\sqrt{a/g}.\]

For \(Y=1\) m and \(X=\pi/2\) m, \(u_f=\pi\) and \(a=0.5\) m. The cycloid time is approximately 0.709 s and the straight track needs about 0.841 s. The endpoint is the bottom of this particular cycloid. Increasing the horizontal offset beyond \(\pi Y/2\) makes the first-arch solution turn upwards before it arrives.

Compare two feasible experiments

The graph plots downward depth against horizontal position. Vary endpoint distance and depth, then predict whether the fastest path has an ascending segment. Read the two calculated times. A physical rolling sphere differs from the sliding particle: rotational kinetic energy multiplies the time by a constant factor if the body rolls without slipping with fixed inertia ratio, whereas frictional loss can alter the optimum shape itself. A track with a prescribed minimum bend radius would also define a different variational problem.

Open this experiment online

Tutorial

Keep track shape geometrically similar and double every length. By which factor does the travel time change?

Work through the solution

The parameter angle is fixed by a length ratio and \(a\) doubles. The time grows by \(\sqrt2\). The straight track time obeys the same scaling. A measured different exponent would suggest another dimensional scale in the apparatus.

Why might a numerical quadrature applied directly in \(x\) at the first sample point report infinite time?

Work through the solution

The release speed vanishes and the track has a vertical tangent. The local time integral remains finite. The cycloid parametrisation cancels both vanishing factors analytically. Evaluating a singular endpoint as an ordinary sample in a trapezoidal rule is an integration error.

How can two paths be compared if a common release mechanism imparts a small initial speed \(v_0\)?

Work through the solution

Energy now gives

\[v(y)=\sqrt{v_0^2+2gy}.\]

Recompute the time functional using that speed and the actual initial condition. Subtracting an arbitrary time offset from both runs cannot undo a depth-dependent modification of travel speed.

Revisit the origin of stationary action and essential boundary data in the moving-constraint chapter.

Mechanics in the laboratory · 5. When can shaking a support stabilise an upside-down pendulum?

A rapidly oscillating pivot can stabilise a pendulum near its normally unstable upright orientation. Develop the slowly varying effective potential, test its assumptions with the full time-dependent equation and compare the observable that each calculation predicts.

Start in the moving frame

Measure angle \(\theta\) from the downward vertical. Let the upward support displacement be \(y_p=a\cos\Omega t\). The effective downward acceleration in the translating frame is \(g+\ddot y_p=g-a\Omega^2\cos\Omega t\). The exact angular equation under these assumptions is

\[\ddot\theta+\left(\frac{g}{L}-\frac{a\Omega^2}{L}\cos\Omega t\right)\sin\theta=0.\]

A simple time average of the coefficient would leave the ordinary pendulum. That would miss the correlation between the rapidly oscillating force and the rapidly oscillating part of the angle. The pivot can do work even though its mean position is fixed. The energy of the pendulum alone is therefore not generally conserved.

Eliminate the fast motion

Write \(\theta=\Theta+\xi\), with slowly varying \(\Theta\) and a small fast correction \(\xi\). In one forcing cycle treat \(\sin\Theta\) as constant. Integrating \(\ddot\xi=(a\Omega^2/L)\sin\Theta\cos\Omega t\) twice for its oscillatory part gives

\[\xi=-(a/L)\sin\Theta\cos\Omega t.\]

Inserting \(\sin(\Theta+\xi)\simeq\sin\Theta+\xi\cos\Theta\) into the exact equation creates a product of two cosines with nonzero mean. Retaining the leading averaged terms yields

\[\ddot\Theta=-\frac gL\sin\Theta-\frac{a^2\Omega^2}{2L^2}\sin\Theta\cos\Theta,\]
\[\frac{U_{\rm eff}}{mL^2}=-\frac gL\cos\Theta+\frac{a^2\Omega^2}{4L^2}\sin^2\Theta.\]

Two approximations entered. The displacement ratio \(a/L\) must keep micromotion small and the drive must be fast compared with the slow angular motion. A large acceleration \(a\Omega^2\) can coexist with a small displacement \(a\); acceleration alone is not the stability criterion.

An observable threshold

Expand about \(\Theta=\pi+\eta\). The averaged restoring coefficient is

\[\omega_{\rm up}^2=a^2\Omega^2/(2L^2)-g/L.\]

A local minimum appears if \(a\Omega>\sqrt{2gL}\). For \(L=0.15\) m and a 60 Hz vertical vibration the threshold amplitude is approximately 4.55 mm. At 6 mm the averaged small-oscillation frequency is about \(1.11\) Hz. A motion sensor attached to the bob will also see the 60 Hz micromotion. Comparing an unfiltered peak with the slow prediction can make the theory seem wrong even when the averaged phase portrait is accurate.

Test the slow approximation against a full integration

Release the bob slightly off the top and change the drive frequency or amplitude. The plot samples the exact forced equation once per forcing period at a fixed phase and compares it with the averaged equation evaluated on the same time grid. The observable is angular deviation from the top, with full turns retained. Small bounded oscillations depend on initial displacement as well as the local curvature; outside the linear range a pendulum can leave the top even when the curvature is positive. Very near the threshold a short record is poor evidence for stability because both a small growth rate and a small oscillation frequency produce slow motion.

Open this experiment online

Tutorial

Two drives have the same product \(a\Omega\) but one uses twice the frequency. What is identical in the averaged model and what differs in the full motion?

Work through the solution

The leading effective potential is unchanged. The higher-frequency drive has half the displacement amplitude and therefore smaller leading angular micromotion. Its separation of time scales is typically better.

Is exactly upright motion evidence that the drive has stabilised the pendulum?

Work through the solution

At \(\theta=\pi,\dot\theta=0\) the sine vanishes for all time. This exact trajectory exists even below threshold. Release with controlled positive and negative tilts and assess whether nearby trajectories remain close.

If the drive is switched off after one second, can the effective potential still be used to predict a permanently stable upright position?

Work through the solution

Once the pivot stops, only the ordinary gravitational potential remains. Integrate the undriven equation using the angle and angular velocity at switch-off. The phase of the rapid motion can affect that initial state.

Compare slow stabilisation here with parametric growth near twice a mode frequency.

Mechanics in the laboratory · 6. When does a smooth circular guide lose contact?

A bead moves inside a vertical circular guide after receiving a known speed at the bottom. Predict whether it turns around, separates from the guide or completes the circle. A normal-force measurement can distinguish these outcomes before a simple top-height energy test can.

Check the constraint force after solving for speed

Use \(\theta=0\) at the bottom, increasing along the rising side. Let \(R\) be the radius of the bead centre's path, \(v_0\) its bottom speed and \(u=v_0^2/(gR)\). The smooth guide does no work. The rise in gravitational energy \(mgR(1-\cos\theta)\) therefore gives

\[v^2/(gR)=u-2+2\cos\theta.\]

This relation applies only while the bead follows the circle and the computed speed is real.

With inward radial direction positive, force balance is

\[N-mg\cos\theta=mv^2/R.\]

Substitution gives

\[\frac{N}{mg}=u-2+3\cos\theta.\]

A guide underneath the bead can push but cannot pull. For \(u<2\) the speed first reaches zero while the contact force is still positive. For \(2<u<5\) the force reaches zero with positive speed at \(\cos\theta=(2-u)/3\). Above that point circular motion would require a negative normal force. For \(u>5\) the bead can remain in contact throughout the circle. At the boundaries \(u=2\) gives a zero-speed, zero-normal grazing turn at the side and \(u=5\) gives marginal contact at the top. A captive slotted carriage or a bead threaded onto a wire has a different constraint and can transmit force of either sign.

Distinguish an energetically accessible top from a feasible trajectory

Let \(R=0.25\) m and choose \(v_0=\sqrt{3gR}=2.71\) m/s. The guide loses contact when \(\cos\theta=-1/3\), or at 109.5 degrees from the bottom. The remaining speed there is \(\sqrt{gR/3}=0.904\) m/s. Raising the initial energy so that \(u=4\) pays the gravitational energy cost to reach the top, but a continuously guided motion still fails the nonnegative force condition earlier. The mechanical-energy and force-balance tests answer different questions.

Exercise · find the lower turning point

For \(u=1\), determine the turning angle and force there.

Work through the solution

Zero speed requires \(\cos\theta=1-u/2=1/2\), hence \(\theta=60^\circ\). The contact force then balances the outward radial component of gravity, \(N=mg\cos\theta=mg/2\). It remains compressive through the turn.

Exercise · size a classroom loop

A bottom speed of 2.0 m/s is available. What is the largest ideal path radius for continuous contact through the top?

Work through the solution

The limiting condition is \(v_0^2=5gR\), so \(R=4/(5\cdot9.81)=0.0815\) m. This is the radius of the bead centre. Rolling friction, rotational kinetic energy or a different channel radius would alter this calculation.

From cut forces to local equilibrium

Engineering mechanics

A support reaction tells you the total force entering a part. To predict what an inclined internal surface carries, keep track of both the orientation of the cut and the direction of the force across it.

A force that depends on the surface you choose

Imagine a small triangular wedge cut out of a thin, slowly loaded plate. Its sloping face has unit outward normal \(\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y)\) and area \(A\). The two faces normal to the coordinate axes have areas \(A n_x\) and \(A n_y\) when both components are positive. Name the internal force per unit area on a face its traction. Opposite faces of the same cut carry equal and opposite tractions. Gravity and acceleration act on volume, which shrinks faster than area as the wedge shrinks. Dividing its force balance by \(A\) therefore gives a relation that no longer contains its size.

\[\mathbf t(\mathbf n)=n_x\mathbf t(\mathbf e_x)+n_y\mathbf t(\mathbf e_y)=\boldsymbol\sigma\mathbf n .\]

The columns of the stress matrix are the two coordinate-face tractions. Their linear combination supplies the force on any inclined face. A small square additionally needs zero net moment. To leading order, the shear forces on opposite faces form two couples of opposite sign and equal lever arm. Their balance requires \(\sigma_{xy}=\sigma_{yx}\) for an ordinary material without internal body couples.

Background · Traction
\[\mathbf t(\mathbf n)=\boldsymbol\sigma\mathbf n\]

Specify the plane normal before projecting the force per area into normal and shear parts. A stress component is not a net force until integrated over an area.

Why a gradient of stress carries a body force

Now use a tiny rectangular element of side lengths \(dx,dy\) and unit thickness. The right-face contribution to horizontal force is \(\sigma_{xx}(x+dx,y)dy\); the left face contributes its negative evaluated at \(x\). Their difference is \(\partial_x\sigma_{xx}\,dx\,dy\) to leading order. Resolve the upper and lower shear tractions in the same way. Add a prescribed horizontal force per volume \(b_x\) and divide by volume. Repeating in the vertical direction produces two independent equations.

\[\partial_x\sigma_{xx}+\partial_y\sigma_{xy}+b_x=0,\]
\[\partial_x\sigma_{xy}+\partial_y\sigma_{yy}+b_y=0 .\]

These equations say nothing yet about how much the material stretches. They can test an assumed stress field before the elastic modulus has even been measured. A candidate must also reproduce the applied boundary tractions. Satisfying the interior equations alone leaves many possible stresses.

Worked example · the grip on a diagonal bonding plane

At a measurement point let \(\sigma_{xx}=60,\sigma_{yy}=20,\sigma_{xy}=10\) MPa. The outward normal is \((0.6,0.8)\). Matrix multiplication gives \(\mathbf t=(44,22)\) MPa. Projection along the normal gives \(0.6(44)+0.8(22)=44.0\) MPa tension. Projection on the unit tangent \((-0.8,0.6)\) gives \(-22.0\) MPa. Reversing the tangent changes the sign of reported shear. Reversing the surface normal reverses the traction vector itself. For a uniform 100 mm² patch the force has components 4.40 and 2.20 kN. Using only normal stress would miss the tangential load that the adhesive must transmit.

Worked example · a specimen with a known stress gradient

Stand a bar upright, support it at its bottom and leave the top free. Use upward \(y\), length \(L\), constant density \(\rho\), and tension positive. The vertical equation reads \(d\sigma_{yy}/dy-\rho g=0\). Integrating from the free top gives

\[\sigma_{yy}=\rho g(y-L).\]

For a 3.0 m aluminium bar of density 2700 kg/m³ the base stress is −79.5 kPa. Its upward support traction is positive because the bottom face has downward outward normal. A uniform cross-sectional area of 200 mm² gives a base reaction of 15.9 N, equal to the weight. The local and global checks involve different quantities but must agree.

Find the angles where the shear traction passes through zero. Compare each with an extremum of the normal traction. Change the sign of the imposed xy shear, sketch the new angles before moving the slider, and check whether the two extreme normal stresses change.

Tutorial · test a candidate before using a material law

In a region with \(x,y\) in metres, propose \(\sigma_{xx}=ax,\ \sigma_{xy}=-ay,\ \sigma_{yy}=0\), where \(a=2.0\) MPa/m. Does the field need a body force? Find the traction at \(x=0.30,\ y=0.20\) m on a face normal to positive \(x\).

Check the balance and the boundary reading

The horizontal divergence is \(a-a=0\). The vertical divergence is zero because the shear has no \(x\) variation. No body force is needed. The face sees the first column of the matrix, \((0.60,-0.40)\) MPa. A traction-free exterior at that location would reject this field even though it satisfies both interior equations.

Further reading · A. F. Bower, Applied Mechanics of Solids, §2.3, internal forces and stress

How a continuum balance becomes a finite-element stiffness matrix

Engineering mechanics

A single bar element can predict an end displacement exactly and still miss the stress field inside. The difference follows directly from the balance it is asked to satisfy.

Turn a differential balance into work against a test displacement

Let a straight small-strain bar of length \(L\) have area \(A\), Young’s modulus \(E\), displacement \(u(x)\) and distributed axial load \(q(x)\) in N/m. Tensile axial resultant is \(N=EAu'\). Force balance on a slice gives \(N'+q=0\). Clamp the left end and prescribe a right-end force \(P\). Multiply the balance by any smooth virtual displacement \(v\) satisfying \(v(0)=0\), integrate along the bar, and integrate the derivative of \(N\) by parts.

\[\int_0^L EA\,u'v'\,dx=P\,v(L)+\int_0^L qv\,dx .\]

The boundary term at the clamp disappears because that displacement is prescribed. The unknown reaction can later be recovered by equilibrium. This formulation requires only first derivatives of trial displacements. Piecewise linear displacements are therefore admissible even though their slopes may jump at internal nodes.

Compute the stiffness rather than memorising it

On an element from \(x=0\) to \(h\), interpolate the two nodal displacements linearly:

\[u=(1-x/h)u_1+(x/h)u_2.\]

Let the test displacement have the same two basis functions. A virtual change of the first or second node gives the corresponding row of the balance. Both derivatives are constant with opposite signs.

\[B=\begin{bmatrix}-1/h&1/h\end{bmatrix},\qquad K_e=\int_0^h B^T EA B\,dx=\frac{EA}{h}\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}.\]

For a constant distributed load, each basis function integrates to \(h/2\), so each node receives equivalent load \(qh/2\). The two rows of stiffness sum to zero. A uniform translation stores no strain energy. At a shared node the neighbouring virtual-work contributions add because both elements refer to the same unknown displacement.

Worked example · compare a nodal value with the stress in a cell

Take a 1 m bar with \(EA=2.0\) MN, uniform \(q=1200\) N/m and free right end. Exact balance integrated from \(N(L)=0\) gives

\[N=q(L-x).\]

Integrating strain from the clamp produces \(u=q(Lx-x^2/2)/(EA)\). The free-end displacement is 0.300 mm. With a single element the free row of the discrete system has stiffness \(EA/L\) and load \(qL/2\), giving the same displacement. Yet its piecewise constant axial force is

\[EAu(L)/L=600\,\mathrm{N}.\]

The exact force ranges from 1200 N at the clamp to zero at the free end. The numerical force represents the mean over the cell.

Worked example · see what doubling resolution changes

Divide the bar into two equal elements. The middle node receives 600 N from both halves together, while the free node receives 300 N. The right element carries 300 N. Equilibrium of the middle node then puts 900 N in the left element. Their extensions are \(900(0.5)/(2\times10^6)=0.225\) mm and 0.075 mm. Nodal displacements agree with the exact quadratic at both nodes. The largest one-sided stress-resultant error within either element is now 300 N instead of 600 N. Comparing only tip displacements would hide this improvement.

Double the number of cells until the force error is below 100 N for the baseline load. Inspect the values on both sides of an element boundary and explain why agreement in tip displacement alone could have ended this refinement study too early.
